The large-scale network of ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray detectors at the Pierre Auger Observatory has begun to yield precise time-resolved data on anisotropies in cosmic-ray arrival directions. By using two distinct methods to identify and quantify these anisotropies, the observation protocols have been established to analyze arrival directions and associated energies of more than 40,000 cosmic rays. Significant anisotropies with right ascension angles around 11.5 and 291.5 hours, and corresponding local sidereal time of 11 hours and 33 hours, have been found at the top of the atmospheric recovery path. These anisotropy patterns are particularly evident among the 8 EeV range, where the left and right hemispheres exhibit opposite orientation. Additionally, the data reveal no anisotropies among the very highest energy group of 7.5 EeV cosmic rays, suggesting that their arrival directions are uniformly distributed. By analyzing the energy dependencies of these anisotropies around the 8 EeV mark, the findings indicate the presence of two distinct components, with one anisotropy decreasing with increasing energy and another increasing with energy. These findings could be attributed to two distinct groups of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays originating either from very local sources or alternatively from two distinct cosmological components. By examining the anisotropy patterns in relation to their right ascension and declination, the data do not indicate any variation in the anisotropy patterns with the atmospheric depth above which these cosmic rays are detected. Finally, the anisotropy patterns are found to persist over a period exceeding 5.5 years, where the local sidereal time and energy around 8 EeV are found specifically to vary with the seasons. Homogenization results for thin layers, whether periodic, almost periodic, or more generally, with quasi-periodic modulations, have been established in the literature. The current paper aims to build upon these existing results by combining them for thin layers with incommensurable modulations. The model problem we consider involves a thin layer, denoted $\omega h$, separated by two domains, $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$, in the space $R^N$, with the distance between these domains, $d(\Omega_1,\Omega_2)$, being an essential parameter influencing the problem. The governing equation, a mixed type of elliptic equation, is formulated on the thin layer, with boundary conditions derived from the nearby domains. Assuming the modulations of the layer and its adjacent domains exhibit Diophantine properties, the model equation can be solved to provide an effective solution, with its high-frequency components being negligible. The resulting solution can be expressed as a low-frequency approximation, with its high-frequency counterpart being exponentially small. The approach employed in this paper involves two main steps: first, the model equation is reformulated as a singularly perturbed problem, with a boundary layer; second, the removal of the high-frequency component, allowing for the construction of the low-frequency approximation, with an error estimate, and the validation of the effective spectrum, along with an estimate of the error, all being facilitated by a compact operator framework. The approach can also be applied to thin layers with boundary operators, as well as stacks of layers, with quasi-periodic modulations. The results obtained can be applied to various physical problems, including superconductivity, superfluidity, and quantum mechanics, providing a useful tool for physicists and researchers working in these fields. The methods employed in this paper are original and can be generalized to other problems, offering a novel approach to homogenization, with the efficiency of this method being confirmed by the provided examples. The paper is organized as follows, with the first section introducing the model problem and relevant assumptions, the second section establishing the high-frequency expansion, the third section constructing the low-frequency approximation, and the fourth section validating the effective spectrum and estimating the error. The conclusion is followed by an appendix providing additional details and generalizing the approach to other types of modulations. The results obtained in this paper confirm that the homogenization theory can be applied to a wide range of situations, with the model considered being a representative example, and the approach employed being flexible and adaptable to various modifications. This study focuses on the critical role of TILs (tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes) in cancer treatment and management. By assessing TILs, healthcare professionals can gauge the potential effectiveness of various treatments and predict patient outcomes. Traditional digitization methods of histopathological samples have proven effective, yet scanning and annotating these images for analysis is a labor-intensive process requiring significant expertise. To address this challenge, our research centers on training a model to analyze H&E (hematoxylin and eosin) images and categorize TILs based on established classification systems such as the Fano classification. Due to the scarcity of large-scale annotated datasets and the need for domain-specific pathology expertise, our approach employs federated learning to facilitate training on distributed datasets. This methodology allows for the development of a more accurate and generalizable model without transferring data. Our results reveal that our approach yields exceptional performance on four distinct pathology datasets, achieving high multi-pathology generalization. Our research is made available through the Pathology image analysis challenge on GitHub, along with the necessary code and configuration to reproduce the study's findings. This study aims to facilitate the development of reliable and efficient image analysis tools for the assessment of TILs, thereby contributing to enhanced cancer treatment and patient care. These research contributions are intended to inspire new ideas and approaches within the broader pathology image analysis community. This research introduces the Evolutionary Pathway Creator (EPC), a universal robot learning method that enables quadrupedal robots to navigate complex environments. Traditionally, robot learning approaches have been confined to specific settings, however our approach enables generalization. EPC employs an evolving neural network that produces movement policies, which are evaluated and refined through reinforcement learning. In contrast to existing methods which often rely on pre-defined action spaces, EPC's evolving structure allows it to generate diverse and dynamic policies. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of EPC in a variety of challenging quadrupedal tasks, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods. Additionally, our findings reveal that EPC can create multiple viable policies, highlighting the benefits of genetic representation for transfer learning and adaptive purposes. Building upon EPC, our study also explores the potential for transfer learning between distinct quadrupedal shapes, showcasing that the evolved policies can be applied to different geometries with minimal adjustments. Guided by the principles of natural evolution, EPC empowers quadrupedal robots to navigate the complexities of real-world environments. The spectra of X-rays emitted by low-brightness AGN in the center of the galaxy NGC 7213 reveal the presence of multiple ionized Fe, a high-energy edge indicative of collisional ionization, and a broad component in the Fe XXV K alpha line. Our data analysis indicates that these features are consistent with a collisionally ionized plasma at temperatures ranging from 0.22 to 0.35 keV, and also coexist with plasma that has been photoionized. A plasma component with similar properties was also detected in the galaxy IC 4325. The origin of the collisionally ionized plasma is unknown, but it may be attributed to either a warm outflow or a steady state subsonic breeze with a mass flow rate in the range of 0.01-0.1 solar mass per year. If this phenomenon is widespread, it could potentially counteract the mass loss associated with relativistic outflows. This paper delves into solving the challenges of switching costs and closed-loop stability when implementing model predictive control (MPC) in complex nonlinear systems with variable operating conditions. To tackle these issues, our approach involves employing a two-part reinforcement learning strategy. Firstly, a novel exploration technique is developed to ensure the MPC's performance during transitions by promoting situations that favor swift recovery. Secondly, a model-free reinforcement learning method is devised to optimize the MPC's configuration, with our current framework capable of addressing up to bi-level reinforcement learning problems. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework through simulations centered on two interconnected nonlinear systems – a continuous stirred-tank reactor and a mechanical system – showcasing the success of our strategy in boosting recovery and configuration outcomes. Notably, our method can operate without an underlying model, highlighting the framework's potential for real-world applications where system models are difficult to obtain. Further analysis reveals that the model-free reinforcement learning approach can yield superior results when compared to existing literature methods. A comprehensive comparison also shows that our two-phase strategy outperforms other state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods in achieving better results. Additionally, our framework exhibits a marked improvement in performance as it approaches the limit of perfect exploration. We anticipate that our framework will serve as a vital reference for developers seeking to enhance reinforcement learning and model-free reinforcement learning methodologies in the future. Furthermore, our findings provide a framework for accurately modeling and approaching the optimal solution in reinforcement learning, thereby facilitating the transfer of this knowledge to the broader MPC community. To conclude, our model-based reinforcement learning approach has been successfully validated across two distinct scenarios, and our associated code has been made accessible via a public GitHub repository for the purpose of facilitating future research and replication of our experimental results. The SiD Sensor detector is a variant of a detector designed for the future ILC, optimized for its high precision and efficiency in identifying particles. Although the original SiD Sensor concept utilized a monolithic design with a high number of readout chips, it had the drawback of being technologically and financially outdated. The modified detector replaces the monolithic design with individual silicon sensors, replacing the sensitive layer with a lightweight, transparent cover to improve detection and reduce particle interaction complexity. Additionally, the modified detector incorporates a newly designed small collection radius with a large acceptance rate, incorporating a trigger system within the innermost detector for reduced data volume and a quicker response time. With improved technology and a simplified design, the modified detector's technical challenges are addressed, and it exhibits enhanced efficiency and performance. This report outlines the design and progress of the modified detector concept.

We have obtained far-ultraviolet images of the globular cluster Ton 2 from data collected with the Cosmic Ultraviolet Telescope on board the Stratospheric Observatory for the Infrared Development during its 2021 flight. These images were captured at a wavelength of 179.4 nm with a spatial resolution of 13.6 arcseconds. We have analyzed the cluster's brightness, finding it at a magnitude of -9.06 and have also detected the presence of the unconfirmed binary system TON 2-1 with a period of 5.442 days. Our analysis, combined with the ground-based spectroscopic survey of the CAPOS program, has allowed us to identify 113 new binary systems in the cluster. It is estimated that this number may only represent 20% of all binary systems in Ton 2 due to detection limitations. We have also explored the distribution of the remaining physical binaries in the cluster, identifying 54 of them. Additionally, our analysis has allowed us to study the rich binary system TON 2-4 with a period of 0.655 days and a companion for the asteroseismic star TON 2-1, with a period of 3.918 days. Our far-ultraviolet imaging technique has provided a more accurate determination of the cluster's velocity dispersion at 5.35 km/s and has allowed us to explore the properties of its stellar mass distribution, finding a slope of 0.20 ± 0.07 for the stellar mass function in the cluster radius. This study has also allowed us to explore the properties of the Galactic bulge's lower metallicity class through the analysis of the cluster's metallicity at [Fe/H] = -1.54 ± 0.03 (1σ) and has found evidence of a significant Galactic bulge's radial velocity of (-20.43 ± 2.05) km/s. This study has also allowed us to explore the properties of the tidal radius of Ton 2 at 16.3 pc and has found evidence of a significant encounter between the cluster and the nearby globular cluster M22. In this study, we employ this technique to model a two-dimensional active nematic system governed by a specific set of equations, ultimately resulting in a novel and detailed description of the system's behavior. This includes the existence of multiple order parameters that govern the nematic's structure and the emergence of robust instabilities through a process called self-replication. The latter is confirmed through numerical simulations, with the added benefit of the prediction of a specific timescale for this phenomenon. This timescale is calculated using the renormalization group approach and is consistent with a complementary simulation. Moreover, the study reveals that certain material properties that were previously considered insignificant actually have a substantial impact on the system's behavior when analyzed through the lens of the renormalization group approach. This leads to a more vibrant and dynamic understanding of active nematics, with potential applications in fields such as cell biology and nematic liquid crystals where the underlying flow plays a crucial role. ReAD employs a segmentation-based method to divide each series into distinct segments both horizontally and vertically. Each segment is then analyzed using the Repeated BIC (ReBIC) measure, which indicates the likelihood of an irregularity within that segment. Following this, ReBIC thresholds are optimized, and a detection strategy is applied to pinpoint the segments containing anomalies. Our proposed framework, ReAD, surpasses existing methods in accuracy and efficiently processes large datasets with minimal computational overhead. Our empirical study encompasses various anomaly types, multiple large-scale datasets, and three distinct detection strategies, which substantiate the effectiveness of ReAD. Ultimately, our framework is designed for real-world applications involving the identification of local irregularities. Its ease of use is illustrated through two custom-case studies, one involving sales forecasting and the other with traffic forecasting. Artificial intelligence's primary objective, addressing complex problems via computation, is hindered by the constraint of operating within a digital framework. Codewalking, an emerging field, aims to develop embodied cognition, utilizing code as the medium for cognitive processes. We conduct a thorough examination into how the gas accretion towards TW Hydrae changes over the course of its 0.1 to 10 years cycle, utilizing data from multiple radio wavelength observations in our study. According to photoevaporation models driven by X-rays from the star, we anticipate a significant decrease in gas accretion rates during the early stages of the cycle. In contrast, MHD disk breeze models, which involve the movement of mass from the disk to the corona, often result in more stable and constant accretion rates. Our analysis reveals that the gas accretion rates in both photoevaporation and MHD breeze models do not match the trends observed in recent TW Hydrae radio observations. However, the MHD breeze model comes closer to replicating the observed trends compared to photoevaporation. To reconcile the discrepancy, we suggest that both processes, including one driven by stellar irradiation and turbulent magnetic forces, might be contributing to the mass flow managed by the disk. A numerical simulation of both disk models, incorporating the effects of both magnetic forces and stellar irradiation, reveals that the mass accretion rates in both the inner and outer disk regions remain relatively consistent, aligning with the observed patterns in TW Hydrae's radio spectra. A brief examination of other T Tauri stars also supports our hypothesis that both the disk breeze and magnetic forces play a role in shaping the observed mass accretion patterns in these young stellar objects. Ultimately, our study underscores the significance of high-angular resolution observations in understanding the internal dynamics and physical processes within the disks of these young stellar objects. This research introduces an innovative method for voicing classification and pitch tracking that doesn't require reference signals from other microphones. Voicing classification involves determining whether audio comes from a voice or not, while pitch tracking identifies the precise moment when audio originates from a voice. Traditional methods rely on the F0 bin-based approach, but it has drawbacks such as being data-hungry, computationally intensive, and sensitive to noise. To address these issues, this study proposes using the Voicing Classification Function (VCF) and Differential Pitch Tracking (DPT) algorithm to classify voicing and track pitch. To enhance noise removal, this approach applies forward-backward Kalman filtering before analyzing the spectrogram. Through experiments using the K-WS dataset, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance, with results showing 2-4% improvement in accuracy compared to the baseline. Notably, the method achieves a voicing classification accuracy of 99.4% and a pitch tracking error rate of 12.96% within 10 milliseconds. To validate its practicality, this study also conducts an acoustical analysis and demonstrates its effectiveness in a real-world application – a home environment. The proposed algorithm is also compared to the state-of-the-art Tandem algorithm, showing 10-20% improvement in accuracy. To facilitate its use in other research, the study provides open-source code and makes the K-WS dataset available. The method's performance is further analyzed using metrics such as the Dice coefficient, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and mean absolute error (MAE). To evaluate its reliability, the study performs a Monte Carlo simulation and presents the mean values. The work's overall structure is then summarized, highlighting the key contributions. To validate its generalizability, the study also conducts an additional experiment using a different dataset – WSJ0. The method performs comparably on this dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness across different scenarios. The study then compares its performance to the state-of-the-art algorithm, DeepVoicing, showing 10-20% improvement in accuracy. To facilitate its use in other research, the study provides open-source code and makes the WSJ0 dataset available. The method's performance is further analyzed using metrics such as the Dice coefficient, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and MAE. To evaluate its reliability, the study performs a Monte Carlo simulation and presents the mean values. The work's overall structure is then summarized, highlighting the key contributions. This study tackles the challenges of solving monotonic inclusion problems, specifically incise problems, by introducing the dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB) algorithm. The incise problem is a broad framework that encompasses various optimization and splitting algorithms as its special cases. Unlike existing methods that require the exact solution of a subproblem, DWIFOB takes a relaxed approach, leveraging the properties of the monotonicity incise problem to obtain an approximate solution. By employing a weighted forward-backward algorithm, DWIFOB efficiently solves the incise problem even in the presence of non-overlapping domains. The results demonstrate the strong convergence of the DWIFOB algorithm. Furthermore, our findings also encompass the forward-reverse algorithm (FOR) and the inertial forward-reverse algorithm (IFOR) as its special cases, which exhibit better convergence performance and higher robustness compared to existing methods in relevant literature. The effectiveness of the proposed DWIFOB algorithm is illustrated through numerical examples. The MATLAB code for the DWIFOB algorithm is available at https://github.com/Chen-Wenlin/dwifob/tree/main/README.md. The research was partially supported by NSFC (No. 11971015). This research focuses on the decentralized training of extractive models for a specific natural language processing task through a novel approach called Communication-Effective Federated Extraction (CEFEX). CEFEX combines the advantages of both federated learning and learning with synthetic data to overcome two key challenges. Firstly, it mitigates the excessive communication requirement of FL by utilizing synthetic data; and secondly, it addresses the loss of domain specificity in data labels using a specialized model, allowing for more accurate adaptation to specific domains with fewer global updates. CEFEX is successfully applied to a prominent NLP model, RoBERTa, on three diverse datasets, achieving synthetic data equivalents with 50% fewer communication rounds and 20% fewer updates on the datasets. Our study also highlights the benefits of incorporating an auxiliary model to preserve task-specific characteristics, which can be valuable in various decentralized training scenarios. Our source code is publicly available.

To obtain optimal performance in complex systems, it is often necessary to balance competing objectives, which can be challenging with unclear trade-offs between these goals. Conventional multi-objective optimization techniques require predefined weightings between objectives, but such weights may not always be known, making this a significant obstacle in many real-world applications. To address this issue, our study focuses on automatically learning objective weights using an iterative process, incorporating prior knowledge to avoid exploring irrelevant or unfeasible solution spaces. We propose the Prior Utility Function Learning algorithm, which learns utility functions by utilizing biased random searches and incorporating prior knowledge through weighted sampling. The effectiveness of this algorithm is demonstrated in two practical scenarios: (1) controlling the balance between exploration and exploitation in decision theory, and (2) managing the trade-off between accuracy and computation time in Bayesian model selection. The algorithm's performance is compared with alternative approaches in several numerical case studies, and further details are available in a publicly accessible Jupyter notebook. The source code for the algorithm is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexanderschmidt1/UtilityFunctionLearning. The empirical results show that our algorithm outperforms existing methods in all tested scenarios, and it can be readily applied to a wide range of problems where multi-objective optimization is required. The algorithm's efficiency and general applicability make it an accessible tool for scientists and engineers to use, and further research will be necessary to identify its specific applications. We introduce a pioneering technique to systematically evaluate the effectiveness of reinforcement learning algorithms in predicting temporal attributes, such as agent representation, action types, and reward structures. Our advanced method enables the creation of artificial datasets that can be used to train attack models, which we refer to as 'Temporal Model Attacks.' The proposed algorithm iteratively generates short sequences of optimal actions to estimate temporal attributes, producing an estimated temporal insight for each attribute. The attack model can then be leveraged to generate adversarial policies that exploit these insights to disrupt reinforcement learning agents. Our experiments demonstrate that RL algorithms like SARSA and Q-learning are susceptible to our temporal model attacks, with the latter yielding more potent adversarial policies. Furthermore, we discover that deep reinforcement learning algorithms like DeepMind Grid World are also vulnerable to our attacks, highlighting the need for enhanced security measures to safeguard these models. The code for our approach is publicly available on GitHub.

Research on Dirac materials has seen an explosive growth in recent years, driven by the potential of harnessing topological properties to transport electric current with minimal resistance. The discovery of Dirac materials in two-dimensional structures has enabled the creation of ultra-conductive 2D Dirac electrics. Current studies on 2D Dirac phases primarily rely on idealized conditions, lacking robust control over Dirac locations. Using the symmetry-protected topology of 2D Dirac phases, our paper presents a new method to place Dirac locations anywhere in a 2D space. We demonstrate this by growing a monolayer of Bi$_2$TeCl, derived from the non-symmorphic wallpaper group, with adjustable chemical properties that allow shifting the Dirac locations across the 2D surface. The Dirac locations can also be completely removed by introducing in-plane strain, thereby providing a level of control unprecedented in 2D Dirac phases. The findings of our theoretical calculations are verified using first-principles simulations, with the results showing that Dirac locations near the Fermi level can be manipulated by modifying the chemical properties or applying strain to the monolayer. The control of Dirac locations could enable the development of 2D Dirac electrics with enhanced electrical conductivity. In reinforcement learning (RL) where an agent's reward is delayed and includes punishment, a risk-aware approach can be applied to achieve more stable policy learning by minimizing long-term damage. While initial risk assessment methods are simple to design, they have limitations in learning optimal policies. To address this issue, we introduce non-stationary risk-aware reinforcement learning that adapts reward estimation and policy learning simultaneously, without assuming the risk function's structure or its stationarity. By modeling risk as a changing vector, we develop a dynamic protocol to manage temporal disconnection and develop an algorithm using deep neural networks, verifying its effectiveness in various games, including those with high complexity. Moreover, we present an identification protocol that accurately estimates risk parameters and provide evidence that our approach is near-optimal and efficient. Notably, our method also improves the separation between safe and hazardous actions, enabling more cautious behavior. By incorporating risk awareness into RL, we demonstrate better performance and more stable policy learning compared to traditional RL approaches. We establish in this work a general framework to derive the platform group for a composition of rational functions when each individual component has a platform group that can be determined. Additionally, we apply this framework to obtain explicit formulas for the platform group of iterative bicritical rational functions, including specific results for the $n$th iterate of $(x^2+1)$ and $(x^3+1)$. Furthermore, we identify the platform group of a particular family of hyperelliptic curves, providing a solution to a question posed by Prendiville and Smyth. Notably, we compute the platform group of $(x^{17}+x)$, a rational function with A-finite Galois group over the rational numbers. Lastly, we outline several related directions for future research. When working with high-dimensional data and unknown error variance, selecting an appropriate prior distribution for regression coefficients in Bayesian linear regression is a complex task. One possible solution is to use the empirical Bayes method, which chooses a prior distribution that maximizes the posterior mixture density. This approach, however, does not guarantee optimal results, particularly in cases where the number of parameters exceeds the number of data points. Researchers have recently established the consistency of the empirical Bayes estimator under the elastic net loss function, but its performance in the presence of varying error variance has not been well characterized. To address this limitation, this study provides a detailed analysis of the empirical Bayes estimator's properties in the presence of heteroscedastic errors. Specifically, it establishes a central limit theorem for the estimator's discrepancy and determines the optimal rate of the estimator's convergence. This rate is influenced by the mustache zone, a region that lies between the 'isotonic' and 'platonic' regions, and is characterized by the parameter space's geometry. Furthermore, this study investigates the empirical Bayes estimator's performance in terms of the false discovery rate and false rejection rate. Finally, supporting simulations demonstrate the estimator's superiority to traditional methods, particularly in cases with varying error variance. Additionally, researchers can use the provided code to reproduce the results and visualize the various regions of the parameter space. Lastly, while this study focuses on Bayesian linear regression, the approach can be extended to fit a wide range of Bayesian models, such as generalized linear models and sparse principal component analysis. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a comprehensive characterization of the empirical Bayes estimator in the context of high-dimensional regression modeling with unknown error variance. By doing so, it sheds new light on the complex interplay between the estimator, the model, and the data, and establishes a theoretical framework that can be applied to a broad range of statistical Bayesian models. Additionally, this study may have implications in other fields, such as neuroscience and genetics, where high-dimensional regression is a critical tool for data analysis. To conclude, this study provides a detailed examination of the empirical Bayes estimator's properties in the presence of heteroscedastic errors, and sheds new light on the complex interplay between the estimator, the model, and the data. To address the anomalous $J/\psi$ production in the proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), we propose a novel approach. Our approach relies on a two-body decay analysis of the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesons, incorporating the most recent data from the LHCb experiment. We also provide a comprehensive review of the historical and ongoing experimental and theoretical research on the subject, including our previous findings published in the journal Physics Reviews D in 2018, which highlighted the distinctive features of the two mesons. Our study involves four possible scenarios, each with its own set of parameters obtained from separate or simultaneous fits of the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesons. We examine the results of these fits, including the signs and consequences of the $\eta$-$\eta'$ interference, in the context of two simple quantum field theory models: one with a single pole and another with two poles, representing the $c\bar{c}$ and $n\bar{n}$ states, respectively. Our study indicates that the signs of the interference are evident in certain energy ranges and that the two mesons can be distinguished based on specific criteria, such as their resonance patterns, relative production rates, and correlation matrices. Our analysis also reveals the potential for the $\eta'$ meson to dominate the $J/\psi$ production in certain scenarios, while the opposite may be true in others, highlighting the complexity and ambiguity of the problem. Our study provides a clear and tangible solution, suggesting that the signs of the interference play a crucial role in distinguishing the two mesons, and that the most suitable choice depends on the specific values of several parameters, which can be determined by considering various possible combinations of the two mesons. Our study addresses two specific concerns highlighted by the LHCb experiment, providing a comprehensive understanding of the distinct features of the two mesons and their behavior in the presence of interference. Our study also sheds light on the historical and ongoing research, highlighting our previous findings and their significance. Our final result is a set of values that can be used to choose the most suitable solution for specific parameters, and our study provides a clear and unambiguous explanation for the observed phenomena at the LHC. Our study is self-contained, and our conclusions are presented at the end. We hope that our study will be useful to the LHCb experiment for its ongoing and future research. By considering the constraints of image coordinates, projection equations, and image reprojections, our approach applies least squares optimization to simultaneously determine 2D object bounding box parameters and 3D object characteristics. In contrast to traditional methods that resolve the pose estimation problem through factorization or factor substitution, our re-evaluation maintains the problem in its complete form and provides an iterative solution that converges to a global optimum. Our method, denoted as Complete Least Squares (CLS), achieves a more comprehensive representation of the pose estimation problem and offers greater computational flexibility than previous approaches. Our results demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of CLS in terms of convergence, precision, and computational complexity, and highlight its applicability for both narrow and wide baseline scenarios. In this note, I want to share a digital version of my laboratory notebook, which I've been updating since 2015. Similar to others in the physics community, my laboratory journal is where I record the detailed history of my experiments, including data, analysis, and results. This digital notebook is built using Markdown and is hosted on my personal website, powered by Jekyll. I've decided to make it publicly accessible in the hope that it may be helpful to others. I'm also using GitHub to manage the repository, allowing me to maintain the digital notebook and track changes. This approach is similar to that of Jeremy Kun, whom I credit for inspiring me. I'm pleased to report that, after eight years, my digital notebook has shown an unexpected level of usefulness, particularly during my current research on ferroelectric domain walls. In this context, I'm using a sluggish approach, updating my notebook only when significant progress is made, to counteract the common misconception that frequent writing leads to better thinking. I'm convinced that this approach has enabled me to make steady progress, often by reflecting on previous experiences and integrating new ideas. I'm confident that this digital notebook has contributed to my success, and I'm now exploring the possibility of using it as a tool to supplement my research output. I'm also interested in understanding the underlying dynamics, which I believe are rooted in the cognitive biases and psychological factors that drive human creativity. In this regard, I'm treating my digital notebook as a cognitive probe, similar to a qualitative research method. I'm convinced that this type of digital notebook can be an invaluable resource for scientists, and I'm willing to share my knowledge with others who may be interested in adopting a similar approach. We propose establishing a comprehensive PDF adjustment theory, integrating various techniques such as PDF scaling, shifting, and reweighting, to create a unified framework. This will enable us to systematically explore the possibilities and limitations of different techniques, optimizing them for specific use cases. Furthermore, this theory will serve as a general framework for developing customized PDF adjustment methods tailored to specific phenomenological requirements, while allowing for a thorough evaluation of their effects on predicted outcomes. To initiate this endeavor, we outline the PDF adjustment theory and examine one instance of customized adjustment, specifically designed to correct theoretical predictions at high and low momentum regimes by incorporating different PDF sets. We then evaluate and compare the performance of several PDF scaling, shifting, and reweighting methods in both the global and factorization senses, along with some novel options, in the context of Higgs production and vector boson pair production predictions. Our study reveals that, under certain conditions, some of these scaling, shifting, and reweighting methods can yield outcomes indistinguishable from each other in predictions, while others may demand the use of adjusted PDFs that differ by orders of magnitude in certain momentum ranges to achieve comparable precision. We hope that this theory and our research will contribute to the development of optimized PDF adjustment methods for a range of processes and encourage further research in this area. We also expect that this theory will be instrumental in informing decisions on the use of PDFs with different coverage in terms of momentum and parton number in global and process-specific analyses. We have made the code for our research publicly available at <https://github.com/PeterBertolini/PDF_adjustment_theory/tree/pdf_adjustment_theory-1.0.0 >. We also note that the PDF sets used in our research, specifically HBND, can be obtained from <https://github.com/PeterBertolini/hbndPDF/tree/hbndPDF-1.0.0 >. When combining multiple long-exposure images to minimize read-time noise, the point spread function (PSF) of the resulting image is not simply the average of the individual PSFs due to the spatially varying weightings applied in the combination process. We present a formula derived from a maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) framework that accurately represents the PSF of a weighted combined image, particularly when the weightings depend on the signal-to-noise ratio (S/N). We provide explicit expressions for the combined image PSF when either a global S/N or a local S/N filter is employed, and demonstrate that the commonly used Gaussian filter produces a combined image with a narrower PSF than that obtained with the S/N-based filter, especially in the presence of many images. However, the S/N-based filter produces more accurate results for the estimated parameters of extended objects, as compared to the global S/N filter, and to some extent, the local S/N filter. We also present a new S/N estimation formula that is applicable even when objects are extended, and derive an expression for the effective area of the telescope that is relevant to the S/N-based filter. Furthermore, we provide a new expression for the variance of the combined image, which is relevant to the global S/N filter, and demonstrate that the commonly used expression is too narrow and does not account for the weightings applied in the combination process. We verify the derived expressions through Monte Carlo simulations, and show that they accurately represent the PSF and variance of the combined image over a wide range of input parameters. This research explores the movement of two-dimensional discs through a narrow, winding passage, examining how their trajectories alternate as they navigate the channel's obstacles. Two distinct types of trapped disc configurations are examined: those that become stuck in a single location, and those that repeat at regular intervals. A set of rules has been developed that allows for the prediction of how disc masses will alternate when the arrangement of these masses follows a predictable sequence. A mass is defined as the difference in size between a disc that has become stuck in the channel and a disc that passes through without getting trapped. Using a tight-binding-like model with a molecular dynamics approach, the electronic density along the Fermi surface of H$_{3}$S has been determined under varying pressure, which shows the emergence of a van Hove singularity (VHS) as pressure nears its critical value of approximately 250 GPa. This VHS significantly enhances electronic interactions and is believed to contribute to the superconducting phenomenon. Our analysis reveals that the pressure at which the VHS appears is highly sensitive to isotopic substitution, with the VHS emerging at lower pressure when lighter isotopes are used. Notably, while hydrogen substitution lowers the critical superconducting temperature (T$_c$), the influence of isotopic substitution on T$_c$ varies based on the specific isotope, with deuterium having a more substantial effect than carbon. Overall, our findings provide a deeper understanding of the role the VHS plays in the superconductivity of H$_{3}$S and highlight the importance of the Fermi surface structure and electronic interactions in achieving high-T$_c$ superconductivity. Lastly, our analysis offers insight into the potential of nitrogen doping in enhancing T$_c$ in these hydride superconductors. Additionally, by studying the phonon spectrum, it has been found that the vanishing of the electron-phonon density of states along the Fermi surface with increasing pressure correlates with the critical superconducting temperature (T$_c$). This observation supports the notion that electronic instability originating from the VHS is the primary driver of superconductivity in these materials. Finally, our analysis on the isotope effect confirms that the T$_c$ degradation following a Murray-McMillan law is an intrinsic property of these hydride superconductors. Murray-McMillan's $\lambda$-value, which represents the relative change in T$_c$ in response to isotopic substitution, was found to be around 4.7 for hydrogen, 3.8 for deuterium, and 3.4 for carbon. A model incorporating the density of states and electron-phonon coupling was used to determine the isotope effect at constant volume and temperature, and the results were consistent with the measured values. Most importantly, our analysis demonstrates that the vanishing of the isotope effect at high pressure in H$_{3}$S is a manifestation of the transition from a metal to an insulator, a phenomenon that has been observed in many high-T$_c$ superconductors. The framework enables several benefits, including reduced data exchange risks and enhanced efficiency in exchanging threat information, as well as the ability to use existing data without needing to be exchanged. The problem of ordering for multiple robotic arms in various configurations is a key challenge in optimal scheduling, with each arm's task sequence influencing the overall efficiency of the ordering. Given the distinct setup of each arm, the ordering problem becomes highly complex, resembling the traveling salesman issue. A proposed solution involves a clustering-based algorithm that groups the arms based on their characteristics, then applies a search technique to arrange tasks in an efficient order. By initially separating tasks within each cluster and determining which clusters need to be visited, the algorithm significantly reduces search complexity. Our technique not only outperforms existing methods but also exhibits flexibility in task definition and robotic arm configuration. A comprehensive evaluation, using simulated and real data from actual production lines, showcases its performance across various scenarios. Additionally, the ordering system includes task dependencies and defines when a task is complete, as well as the timing and duration of each operation. A comparative study against other algorithms and a detailed analysis of our approach are provided, with further details on how to optimize task sequences based on specific conditions of the multi-arm configuration. The technique is currently available as part of the MultiARM package on GitHub. However, its design allows for a high degree of scalability, making it adaptable to a range of scenarios and arm configurations. The experimental data, including results from our evaluation, can be found on this repository. The findings of our study are also presented in a research paper published in the Journal of Intelligent Manufacturing. The domain of optimal scheduling within multi-arm configurations has received relatively little attention, with most studies either ignoring task sequences or adopting simple, first-come-first-served approaches. Graph Neural Networks have achieved significant success in various graph classification tasks. However, many real-world datasets come with a constraint of having only one labeled node for each graph, which poses a problem for models that rely on node features. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a method that utilizes the model's self-supervised capabilities to assign meaningful labels to unmarked nodes within a graph. This allows us to leverage the node's features to represent the entire graph, making it feasible for pseudo-tagging. Our approach entails two stages: initially selecting nodes that provide the most accurate predictions based on the model's performance on unmarked nodes, and then assigning labels to unmarked nodes based on the top-ranked nodes' characteristics. Our method has been successfully integrated into multiple graph classification models and has shown improved performance on 4 benchmark datasets, with a significant reduction in the impact of label limitations. Previous studies by Deift, Jenkins, and Klein have established that, under these conditions, the zero of $f(z)$ follows a path governed by the Airy equation, resulting in the renowned Ustinenko-Ushakov junction condition. Our investigation seeks to elucidate the underlying mathematical framework that generates this condition. The implementation of AI systems in high-stakes settings poses significant risks that have already materialized in various forms, including errors, manipulations, and malicious actions. To mitigate future AI-related mishaps, it is essential to document and collect information about past incidents. This paper proposes the creation of the AI Incident Repository (AIR), an comprehensive database of AI system failures, including failure modes, causes, and consequences. By maintaining the AIR, we aim to track the progression of AI-related incidents over time, identify emerging patterns, and develop more effective prevention strategies as the field continues to evolve. This proposal is accompanied by a thorough investigation of potential methods for establishing and maintaining the AIR, as well as an initial population of notable AI system failures known as the AI Failures Dataset (AIFD). This dataset comprises 234 instances of AI system failures, spanning over a decade and categorized into major domains, including self-driving vehicles, medical diagnosis, and energy management systems. Our analysis of the AIFD reveals that while some domains are still relatively new in terms of AI system deployment, the underlying risks remain consistent, prompting the creation of the AIR. Ultimately, the AIR and AIFD can serve as valuable resources to inform discussions about the societal implications of AI, foster collaboration among AI developers, and drive research focused on enhancing AI safety and reliability. This work has been inspired by the Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS), a renowned safety incident repository that has significantly contributed to the advancement of aviation technology and human factors. As our reliance on AI grows, it is crucial that we establish a similar safety incident repository to avoid and mitigate recurring AI-related failures in the future. This research will be made available on our website: https://ai-incidents.org. This material will be updated regularly to maintain the accuracy of the AI Incident Repository (AIR) and provide a clear research vision. Moreover, we will outline our research approach, describe the population of failure instances, analyze the current state of research, and highlight the substantial benefits and challenges associated with maintaining the AIR. This research will address various questions such as What constitutes an AI system failure? How can we verify the incidence of a failure? What are the potential uses of the AIR? What difficulties may arise in maintaining the AIR, and how can we overcome them? This research will serve as a foundation for further exploration of the AIR and will inform our efforts to establish and maintain the incident repository. As a starting point, we will present the AI Failures Dataset (AIFD), a collection of 234 documented AI system

The first method employs the differential reflection spectrum to determine the phase, while the second method utilizes the demodulation of a Michelson interferometer to achieve the same goal. Both methods have the advantage of not requiring rapid switching or complex data analysis, making them particularly suitable for setups with slow-response emitters and limited measurement times. The implementation of these techniques has the potential to facilitate accurate quantum sensing and contribute to the development of precise sensing technologies. Assembling the components of a complete genome from fragmented, short DNA sequences is a time-consuming process that recently became more manageable with the advancement in long-read sequencing technologies. A widely used approach, graph-based assembly, creates a de Bruijn graph from the sequenced data, and using a k-mer string as input, simultaneously allows multiple processors to contribute to the assembly by traversing and shortening edges in the graph. However, since the graph is stored in a compressed format on a single node, it must be split into equal parts among the processors and processed in each node, resulting in the bottleneck of the assembly process. In this study, we present a new algorithm that allows direct assignment of graph parts to any available processor, and along with other changes, significantly improves the overall assembly speed on large-scale computing clusters. The algorithm's effectiveness is confirmed through experiments using the graph-based assembly tool wtdbg2 on various sequencing data sets. The results show that the new algorithm can increase assembly speed by a factor of up to 6.4 for single-machine configurations and up to 3.3 for cluster configurations with 64 processors, and even more so when combined with other optimizations. We introduce an innovative technique for isochronous mass spectrometry that utilizes the $B\rho$-defined ion optical system. This system merges the principles of isochronous focusing with those of the matrix and lets multiple ion beams with varying magnetic rigidities be measured simultaneously at the same point. We detail the design and physics underlying this new method, which we implement at the SHICAT system and use to measure the mass-to-charge ratio of several short-lived nuclei, including $^{46}$Cr, $^{50}$Fe, $^{54}$Ni, and $^{58}$Ni. Our results demonstrate the high accuracy of this new method, which is especially suited for making mass measurements of highly charged and short-lived nuclei. Furthermore, we discuss the potential for using this technique to make mass measurements at low-energy beam lines and to increase the frequency and duration of excursions in the beam, thereby greatly enhancing the system's sensitivity and scope. We outline a plan to use the technique for a comprehensive series of precision mass measurements at the SHICAT system. We also discuss the prospects for using this technique at the Facility for Antiproton Injection and Dubna Gas-filled Recoil Separator, while highlighting the difficulties posed by the beam's low yield, charge state mix, and limited residence time, as well as the challenges of performing high-accuracy mass measurements of highly charged nuclei. We propose a range of possible modifications to the FGDRS and DFS to overcome these obstacles and enable the performance of precision mass measurements using the $B\rho$-defined isochronous technique. We provide an in-depth evaluation of the potential for using the $B\rho$-defined isochronous technique to make precise mass measurements over a broad spectrum at the FGDRS and DFS. This role can potentially be filled by procedure monitoring, an aspect of process mining. However, existing monitoring methods are limited in that they may fail to detect all deviations from a prescribed procedure. In an attempt to rectify this issue, we introduce a new approach to procedure monitoring, one that guarantees the detection of every deviation from a given template procedure. This method involves representing procedures as finite path automata and comparing them with the actual process executions recorded in a log. Our approach can be applied to both structured and unstructured procedures but comes with a heightened time and space complexity, making it more suitable for smaller procedure profiles. In particular, procedure-related data is stored in a dedicated memory section, and the overall complexity depends on procedure properties rather than the available memory. While this method may not be practical for very large procedures, it offers a valuable theoretical foundation and provides a useful method for verifying the correctness of procedure-based systems, especially those with limited procedural complexity. Additionally, this foundation can be expanded to accommodate more sophisticated procedures by incorporating additional techniques, such as partitioning and representing procedures by finite-state machines. By incorporating our method, developers can ensure their system operates in accordance with a predefined procedure, while also uncovering any unconsidered implementation details. In doing so, our approach elevates procedure monitoring from a mere diagnostic to a prescriptive tool. In a broader context, our work contributes to the broader fields of formal methods, process mining, and runtime monitoring. By merging the strengths of these areas, our approach offers a more comprehensive solution, one that can effectively detect all procedure-related issues and provide valuable insights for procedure-based systems. Customized search results can skew data analysis, making it essential to account for any potential biases when studying Web search outcomes. Our investigation focused on two critical aspects: how often customized search results occur and how these events affect the overall ranking distribution. To address these questions, we developed a novel approach, combining both theoretical and experimental components. Firstly, we created a simplified model to estimate the probability of observing customized ranks. Our analysis revealed that this probability declines exponentially with the depth of the search hierarchy. Experimentally, we analyzed over 1.8 million search queries across 20 distinct domains and found that our theoretical framework accurately predicts the probability of observing customized ranks 94.8% of the time. Furthermore, we demonstrated that failing to consider customized ranks leads to underestimating the tail of the rank distribution by as much as 9% and the mode by as much as 5%. Our study provides quantifiable insights into the influence of customized search outcomes and offers recommendations for researchers to mitigate these effects in their own analyses. Additionally, we provide an online tool for quickly assessing the likelihood of encountering customized ranks on specific search terms. Overall, our findings underscore the importance of acknowledging and addressing the potential biases inherent in Web search outcomes to ensure more accurate research conclusions. (C) 2023. Radiomics analysis in CT scans has shown significant potential for improving the accuracy of disease diagnosis and treatment monitoring by enabling detailed characterization of tissue heterogeneity. However, the accuracy of radiomics analysis is heavily dependent on accurate image segmentation, which can be time-consuming and labor-intensive. In this study, we investigated the feasibility of using a deep learning-based approach to automate the segmentation of the gastrointestinal tract in CT scans. By leveraging a large dataset of 20,020 CT scans, we developed and validated multiple models for the automatic segmentation of the liver, pancreas, and gastrointestinal tracts. The results showed that our models exhibited high accuracy, with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve exceeding 0.95 for all targets. Furthermore, the application of these models in clinical settings enabled the characterization of gastrointestinal tumors and benign lesions in the upper and lower gastrointestinal tracts. Notably, the models demonstrated excellent generalizability across different institutions, with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranging from 0.94 to 0.97 for independent validation datasets. In conclusion, our deep learning-based approach has shown promise for accurately detecting and characterizing gastrointestinal tumors and lesions in CT scans through automatic segmentation of the gastrointestinal tract. This novel application has the potential to enhance the clinical utility of CT-based radiomics analysis. With ongoing advancements in artificial intelligence, we anticipate that our approach will contribute to the development of more accurate and personalized cancer diagnosis and treatment. In the future, this model will be integrated into a clinical decision support system to facilitate the clinical evaluation of CT-based radiomics analysis, ultimately leading to improved patient outcomes. Compositional data that represent the coherent combination of multiple components cannot be effectively analyzed using common statistical methods without alteration because of the inherent zero-sum property.  By transforming these data into logarithmic ratios of each component, the resulting variables become independent and identically distributed, making them usable for exploratory and confirmatory data analysis.  This work focuses on the fundamental mathematical aspects, specifically for datasets with two to four components, and highlights the relationships between the variables via their mathematical interpretations and associated statistical properties, as well as best practices for visualization and interpretation using established statistical methods.  The underlying mathematical concepts are original, whereas the approaches to analysis and interpretation are influenced by the compositional data analysis approach of Aitchison and colleagues.  This approach is presented in a straightforward, elementary manner, suitable for entry-level students in statistics or data analysis courses.  The associated R functions and example data are also provided.  This material can be effectively utilized for a one-semester course or as supplementary reading for a statistics or data analysis course.  The flow of this content can be altered to accommodate instructors' preferences.  The companion R code is publicly accessible at <https://doi.org/10.6084/m1.fw-sy4974g>.  The corresponding LaTeX document containing the text and mathematical expressions can also be obtained from the same repository.  This content can be modified to accommodate various presentation styles.  The material has already been utilized in multiple academic settings, and I welcome any suggestions for further improvement.  Please feel free to reach out to me at jianjiaopeng@gmail.com.  I am more than happy to provide any necessary assistance.  I have also provided a video explaining the concepts in detail, available at <https://youtu.be/6h4yj4x9B9Q>.  I have received numerous inquiries about the content, and I have responded to these inquiries, making the content publicly available, as exemplified by a recent email (see arl3940.pdf).  This content has been endorsed by multiple prominent statisticians, as demonstrated by the letters arl3941a and arl3941b.  I have also been awarded the 2022 Theodor Haas Award for an outstanding contribution to the advancement of statistical education.  This content has been translated into Chinese, as shown in arl3942.  I have provided a public R answer explaining the concepts, available at <https://doi.org/10.6084/m1.fw-sy4974g>.

The deserts of sub-Saturn mass exoplanets, where few or no small planets are found, have been identified in certain regions of parameter space from radial velocity measurements. Previous studies have suggested these deserts may exist around low-mass stars similar to the Sun, based on data from the CORALIE/HARPS sample. However, a re-examination of this data revealed no indication of such a desert around low-mass stars. By using Bayesian inference, the probability of discovering additional planets in the CORALIE/HARPS radius range and orbiting inner planets was determined. As a result, the probability of a sub-Saturn mass star like the Sun having few or no inner planets was found to be very low, specifically less than 0.7% at a 95% confidence level. The findings of this study imply that the abundance of small inner planets around low-mass stars is significantly higher than previously suggested by the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity sample. Consequently, the sample may be biased, potentially due to an over-abundance of planets in the radial velocity survey or a difference in stellar metallicity. The discrepancy between the probabilities of discovering additional inner planets and the observed galaxy demographics, which indicate a transition from a planet-rich to a planet-poor population around stars with masses between approximately 0.1 and 0.4 solar masses, remains unexplained. Future surveys, such as the PLATO mission, will have the necessary sensitivity and volume to resolve the uncertainty surrounding the sub-Saturn mass desert and inner exoplanet abundance around low-mass stars. Additionally, differences in stellar metallicity may affect the presence or absence of the desert around low-mass stars, such as those with very low metallicity, where no inner exoplanets are typically expected to be detectable through radial velocity measurements. As a result, the volume and sensitivity required to distinguish between the no-inner-exoplanet and no-desert scenarios around low-metallicity stars will be significantly lower than for metal-rich stars, such as the Sun. Therefore, a dedicated, small-scale photometric or spectroscopic survey of a relatively small, low-metallicity sample volume of stars may be sufficient to determine whether the no-inner-exoplanet or no-desert hypothesis is correct. As a result, the no-inner-exoplanet or no-desert hypothesis surrounding low-metallicity stars can be tested with a relatively small, low-budget survey. To effectively handle long-term dependencies, attention-based models often employ multiple layers. However, excessive use of additional attention layers can lead to performance degradation and over-complication of the model. 

Our proposed mutual knowledge enhancement technique allows existing attention layers to learn and share information more effectively without adding extra layers. 

Through mutual knowledge enhancement, models can better focus on crucial information and restrict unnecessary attention to irrelevant details. 

As a result, models can achieve comparable performance to their hierarchical counterparts with a reduced number of attention layers and equivalent training efficiency. 

Our technique is versatile and can be applied to various attention mechanisms, including multiplicative and additive types. 

Additionally, it enhances the model's robustness by limiting the distribution of attention weights. 

Experimental evaluations on various datasets and attention mechanisms substantiate the efficacy of our proposed method. 

The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/whaiwhai/MKE.

We outline a simple and powerful image feature that captures the patterns of an image volume, allowing for accurate detection of corresponding structures between volumes, even in the presence of significant distortions. We further demonstrate that these features can be effectively used to register volumetric images, yielding a versatile and flexible method. As an extension to this idea, we also introduce a more sophisticated feature that takes into account the inherent symmetry of an object, enabling the registration of asymmetrical features and pushing the alignment precision to an average error of 1.4 millimeters. To validate our methods, we conducted experiments using a public dataset containing CT scans of prostates, as well as simulations to assess our features' performance under controlled conditions. Our results reveal that the proposed symmetrical feature offers the most accurate alignment among all evaluated techniques. With further development, this technique has the potential to streamline clinical procedures such as radiotherapy and surgical planning, enabling more efficient use of existing treatments and treatments in development. Recent advances in monocular depth estimation have shown that pre-training approaches using this task can enhance the performance of other computer vision tasks. Nevertheless, the conventional wisdom is that semantic segmentation can deliver superior pre-training than depth estimation due to the segmentations direct relationship with pixel-level labeling, a crucial component of many computer vision applications. In this study, we challenge this assumption by presenting evidence that depth estimation might actually offer advantages over semantic segmentation pre-training, particularly when pixel-level labeling is not required. Our findings are grounded in the observation that depth estimation is an inherently continuous prediction output, whereas semantic segmentation is a categorical prediction. Moreover, we observe that depth estimation can facilitate the development of supervisory signals that are absent in semantic segmentation. To validate our claims, we conduct a comprehensive experimental evaluation that compares the pre-training effects of depth estimation and semantic segmentation on three independent tasks: semantic segmentation, domain adaptation, and stereo estimation. Our results indicate that depth estimation consistently yields superior pre-training outcomes in all examined scenarios, underscoring the significance of task selection in pre-training approaches. Additionally, we propose a novel technique that leverages depth estimation targets to produce continuous supervisory signals for stereo estimation, achieving superior performance when compared to traditional methods. Developing an automated system to generate engaging stories about time-series data from various domains has remained a complex challenge in the field of natural language generation. Existing neural story generation models often rely on domain-specific knowledge, which can result in stories tailored to a single domain, or else produce generic yet unengaging stories lacking essential details. This paper introduces TCube, a novel neural story generation model that can adapt to any domain while producing engaging stories. TCube employs a novel cube structure, featuring a event selector, event enricher, and post-processing component to sequence events into a coherent narrative. Our approach effectively captures long-term dependencies in the time-series data and incorporates domain-agnostic semantic features to enrich events, as supported by our experiments across three distinct domains: medical condition narratives, earthquake reports, and sports game events. Our results demonstrate that TCube produces stories with greater engagement, higher coherence, and more interesting content compared to stories featuring only selected events or generic post-processing alone. Our source code is available at https://github.com/aleksandr-matveev/TCube. Our generated stories can be found at https://tcubestories.github.io/. This study examines the practice of professionals connecting their online presence across multiple platforms, focusing on the popular coding community Stack Overflow. Our analysis reveals that users share their professional details across external platforms, such as LinkedIn and GitHub, at a higher rate on Stack Overflow than on other online forums. At the same time, we found that only a small percentage of Stack Overflow users share their external platform links, highlighting a need for more research on the motivations behind linking these accounts. Our investigation also explores the relationship between user characteristics and the number of external connections shared, revealing that older developers and those with more work experience are more likely to share these connections. Interestingly, we found no significant correlation between the number of code snippets shared and the practice of linking external platforms. This research contributes new knowledge to the field and paves the way for further study on the benefits and drawbacks of publicly linking multiple online accounts. Our findings can also inform developers and programmers on the best practices for managing their online presence across different platforms. Additionally, we highlight potential security risks associated with publicly linking multiple accounts, which may result in compromised account security. Based on these outcomes, we propose several recommendations to improve online security, such as using distinct passwords across all platforms and regularly monitoring account activity. These recommendations can benefit not only coders but also anyone with an online presence. Our study also raises questions for future research, such as the impact of public account linking on online security and the potential loss of personal data. Furthermore, we suggest investigating the benefits and drawbacks of public account linking, which may result in a more comprehensive understanding of the practice and its implications for online privacy and security. Our data is available on GitHub for other researchers to build upon our findings and conduct additional analysis. Our article also includes a section on replication, which outlines the steps for replicating our study. To create a comprehensive patient record, clinical researchers need to analyze and aggregate information from various medical sources, but often struggle due to inconsistent recording practices. One crucial step in this process is signing medical records, which are typically recorded in a specific and often machine-readable format. However, different hospitals and systems often use distinct software and guidelines to capture these records, resulting in incompatible formats that hinder automated processing and integration. To address this challenge, our study proposes a novel approach called Sign Event Extraction, which aims to extract meaningful information from signing records and translate it into a standardized format applicable across multiple systems and institutions. Building on the success of domain generalization techniques in other fields, we develop a new approach specifically for sign event extraction, effectively transferring knowledge from one domain to another and enabling accurate extraction even in domains unrelated to the original domain. Experimental evaluations on real-world data from two major hospitals demonstrate the outstanding performance of our proposed method, which significantly surpasses traditional and deep learning-based models that rely on supervised training. Notably, our approach also exhibits excellent generalization capabilities, extracting over 90% of relevant information from unseen domains while maintaining an impressive extraction accuracy of over 90% in those domains. Additionally, our proposed method shows remarkable adaptability, accurately extracting information from domains with minimal to no labeled data and even extracting over 80% information from a domain with no labels from a different hospital. These remarkable outcomes open up new avenues for using signing medical records to establish patient records, and our proposed method can be applied to other fields as well, given its generalizability across domains. To facilitate the reproduction of our results and provide a public knowledge base for sign event extraction, we also release our implemented code, as well as a publicly available sign event extraction dataset containing over 13,000 signing records from two major hospitals. This comprehensive sign event extraction dataset can be accessed via our project website at the given link. In the future, our proposed method could be applied to other domains such as transaction records, and our developed sign event extraction dataset could be expanded to include more domains as well. To ensure the transparency of our work, we also provide the index of our sign event extraction dataset, which can be accessed via our project website at the given link. Our proposed method is currently composed of three major components, each of which is designed to capture specific aspects of signing medical records. These components are then combined to form a robust and generalizable sign event extraction framework, which is capable of extracting information from signing records in various domains. According to this model, these transitions result from a previous transition's residual energy, which then undergoes a more efficient, yet less conventional $\beta$-decay process. Using this interpretation, the transition can be seen as a sequence of two $\beta$-decays with a gap in between. This prediction aligns with observations found in nuclei such as $^{46}$Cr and $^{50}$Fe, where the presence of intermediate transitions has been detected. Furthermore, this model suggests the presence of intermediate transitions in $^{54}$Fe, which has yet to be observed. Additionally, the model has implications for zero neutrino double-beta decay processes, where the presence of intermediate transitions could potentially impact measurement accuracy. Finally, a list of nuclei with potential intermediate transitions has been compiled based on the proposed model's criteria. These nuclei include $^{38}$S, $^{42}$Cr, $^{46}$V, $^{50}$Mn, $^{54}$Cr, $^{58}$V, $^{62}$Mn, and it is anticipated that further research will confirm their presence. Lastly, the model's double-beta decay applications could be explored in experiments at the LHC, where researchers could utilize magnetic separation to identify ions of these nuclei. Ultimately, the proposed model may contribute to a deeper understanding of the behavior of these heavy ions. Finally, the impact of the irremovable mass term on the Bethe-Salpeter equation and the holomorphic gauge coupling will be discussed, with an emphasis on the implications for the oligomerization of quark bound states. The findings will be represented through the infrared equivalence principle, with the $SO(N_c)$ theories paired against the $SU(N_q)$ theories, where $N_q$ represents the number of quark flavors. To gain deeper insights into random forests, we developed a novel approach called Disentangled Assignment Curves (DACs), which reveal how individual trees within a random forest contribute to the model's predictions. Each DAC is a unique curve representing a tree's prediction contribution for a specific sample, much like the famous LDA curve in supervised learning. Our DAC method surpasses existing alternatives in terms of computational efficiency, accuracy, and interpretability, yielding a $6\times$ improvement in computational time. Building on DACs, we introduced Enhanced Trees, a new framework that utilizes DACs for selecting the most informative trees and pruning unnecessary ones, resulting in a $15\%$ improvement in computational efficiency without compromising accuracy. Our methods were thoroughly evaluated using diverse datasets and scenarios, showcasing their effectiveness and versatility. DACs are now freely available on GitHub under the name Disentangled Assignment Curves, along with accompanying documentation. Furthermore, a related R package called DACs is also being developed.
