In recent times, there has been an increased interest in using Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) for secure machine learning operations. A major limitation of current TEE-based solutions is that model and data are typically isolated from each other, necessitating expensive data uploads to the TEE for inference processes, and hindering the efficiency of training procedures, which often require repeated data transformations. This research proposes an approach called Flatee that enables secure cross-party collaborative machine learning by harnessing the functionality of TEEs in conjunction with secure protocols. Notably, Flatee distinctively integrates three key features: (1) a novel efficient data transformation technique within TEEs; (2) a novel secure protocol that facilitates secure model parameter exchange between parties without revealing the contents; and (3) a novel secure protocol for multi-party ML training that is both efficient and secure. Through comprehensive evaluation, our findings illustrate the superiority of Flatee over state-of-the-art baselines in terms of execution speed and training efficiency. Specifically, our results show that Flatee achieves a training efficiency improvement of up to 4.97 times and an average execution speed improvement of up to 17.91 times compared to the best existing solution. Furthermore, our findings also demonstrate that Flatee is capable of achieving accurate ML model results with comparable performance to that of standard ML models, particularly on datasets such as CIFAR10 and ImageNet. Ultimately, our research showcases that Flatee is an advanced TEE-based solution that addresses the previously acknowledged limitations of ML training efficiency and security via collaborative learning across multiple parties. Our findings highlight that Flatee is capable of achieving significant improvements in both security and efficiency while maintaining robust security against complex attacks. Consequently, we believe that Flatee presents a viable solution for securely and efficiently facilitating ML training among multiple parties. Our research includes a publicly accessible online demonstration and a detailed repository with implementation details, thereby enabling reproduction of our results by other researchers and advancing the knowledge in this domain. Our research also includes two additional papers that provide a deeper examination of Flatee from distinct perspectives, thereby presenting a more comprehensive understanding of the research. Specifically, the first additional paper delves into the security evaluation of Flatee via rigorous testing of various security vulnerabilities while the second additional paper presents a comparative analysis of Flatee against a collection of existing ML training solutions. Collectively, our research comprises three papers that present a novel ML training framework called Flatee, which we believe will contribute positively to the advancement of secure ML training among multiple parties. The cleanup operation for the Chernobyl nuclear disaster necessitated the deployment of a diverse array of equipment, resulting in a vast terrain to cover and an assortment of tasks that required efficient execution. To address this challenge, a range of industrial robots and their combinations were used to accomplish various objectives. Given the limited visibility and hazardous environment, human operators required training to safely operate these robots from a distance. Traditionally, this involved extensive, on-site instruction; however, with the advent of autonomous and partially autonomous robots, the need for costly, site-specific training has significantly decreased. This paper presents an innovative approach to remotely operating industrial equipment using virtual reality interfaces, enabling manufacturers to create standardized training programs that can be delivered digitally. By leveraging this technology, operators can develop the necessary skills using the same virtual interface, regardless of their location, and can hone their abilities in a risk-free digital environment. To illustrate the effectiveness of this methodology, the paper outlines the results of a comprehensive evaluation of a PR2 robot operator, comparing the performance of traditionally trained operators with those trained using the virtual reality platform. Key outcomes of this study include the establishment of a correlation between the number of virtual training sessions and the level of proficiency, as well as the discovery that, following just eight virtual training sessions, the performance of the remotely operated PR2, as manned by a virtually trained operator, equaled that of an operator with extensive on-site experience. This research has far-reaching implications for a wide range of applications, including space exploration, where operators may need to control robots from a significant distance, and industrial settings, where the workload may be distributed across multiple machines. To expand the scope of this study, supplementary material is available that includes videos demonstrating the assessment of operators' skills in navigating through 3D environments using VR, as well as the creation of a standard map system to facilitate comparison of the performance of human operators. This paper introduces a method called Timeloops to automate the creation of system call filters for containerized applications. By learning the patterns of system call behavior during specified time intervals, Timeloops generates filters to confine a service's operation to a designated timeframe. Our approach requires minimal manual involvement and can be scaled for use with large-scale distributed systems, as well as with services that have not been previously evaluated in terms of system call activity. To demonstrate the efficiency of Timeloops, we have created a prototype based on the Linux seccomp library and have tested it by applying system call filters to various services, including a set of seven microservices that have established reputations in the field of distributed applications. Our results show that Timeloops is capable of producing system call filters that accurately capture a service's behavior with high precision, and that these filters can be used to enhance system security by limiting a service's access to certain system resources. Our research also highlights the potential for Timeloops to be used in a wide range of security applications, such as detecting malicious activity and preventing system attacks, while also providing a framework for future research in these areas. Additionally, we have identified areas for future improvement and have developed a framework for evaluating and validating system call filters, which we refer to as Valiloops. Our findings and prototype implementation of Timeloops, as well as Valiloops, can be accessed via an online public repository. By examining the mass distribution of stars in galaxies with a supermassive black hole, the relationship between star formation and black hole mass can be understood. Previous studies have focused on the mass discrepancy gap (MDG) to understand this interaction, but the concept has been poorly defined, leading to different interpretations. In an effort to clarify this understanding, the idea of the MDG is reevaluated, and a new approach called the Stellar Arrangements framework is developed to describe the mass distribution of stars accurately. The framework consists of multiple phases, each representing the mass distribution of stars, and is based on the simple stellar population's spectral luminosity distribution model. The results of applying this framework reveal that the presence of a supermassive black hole leads to star formation that is both more abundant and has a higher average mass at low rates, indicating a dual role in galaxy development. The framework's application also shows that the transition from one phase to another is influenced by the galaxy's mass, and the time required to complete this transition is directly proportional to the galaxy's mass. Furthermore, the framework's results suggest that the mass under way increases in a power-law relationship with the logarithmic mass of the galaxy, a relationship known as the Kennicutt-Schmitt law. This study documents the history and application of sundials in Indonesia and explores their potential as a cultural heritage preservation tool. As a significant astronomical instrument, sundials not only provide educational value but also offer a unique connection to local cultural histories that can be utilized to trigger community memories. Our research approach is divided into two components. First, we gather information about sundials through literature review and field research, recording their locations and photographing them against the local skyline to capture their spatial and cultural contexts. Our sundial survey database also includes data on astronomical declinations, which can be used to monitor celestial changes and engage local communities in timekeeping traditions. Our fieldwork spans 25 provinces, and we present our findings in an online platform recording Indonesia's sundial history, complete with community memories and photos showcasing the sundials' spatial relationships with their surroundings. Our ultimate goal is to empower local communities to become the custodians of Indonesia's sundial heritage, preserving their histories and promoting the transfer of traditional knowledge to the next generation. Our approach may serve as a model for other countries with sundial heritage, and we envision the development of a global network centered on the International Solar Timekeeping Community, where members can access our online database and find information on best practices for recording and preserving sundials. Our methodological innovation lies in combining astronomical and cultural documentation, and we hope that our study will inspire other researchers to collaborate with local communities in preserving their shared cultural heritage, as well as the celestial memories embedded in Indonesia's sundial clock. This study presents a novel approach to 2D data and power networking by incorporating Intellect Reflecting Surface (IRES) into D2D communication designs. To address the challenges of power consumption and interference in existing D2D systems, we are introducing a dual-function IRES that can handle data exchange and power transfer over D2D links. We develop an optimization framework to maximize the sum of individual users' information transfer rates and power transferred rates, subject to interference, power consumption, and reserve power constraints. To solve this complex problem, we propose two algorithms: the first is a suboptimal solution using a multi-blockage approach, and the second is a iterative algorithm in conjunction with the alternating direction method of multipliers. We conduct extensive simulations to evaluate the performance of our proposed algorithms and validate their effectiveness. Furthermore, we examine the optimal values of key system parameters that influence the network performance. Our study demonstrates that the proposed algorithms can achieve substantial gains in sum information transfer and power transferred rates, and these rates can be significantly improved by adjusting system parameters such as the number of IRES blocks, the IRES blocksize, the IRES block spacing, the IRES block gain, and the IRES gain. We also observe that the proposed algorithms can yield near-optimal performance even at high system parameter values. Notably, the suboptimal solution algorithm exhibits a low computational complexity of $4N_{\mathcal{B}}^{3}+3N_{\mathcal{B}}^{2}+2N_{\mathcal{B}}+1$, where $N_{\mathcal{B}}$ represents the number of IRES blocks. We anticipate that the findings of this study will serve as a valuable reference for the design of IRES-assisted D2D communication systems. These results may also be extended to various other areas such as wireless power transfer and non-terrestrial communications. Additionally, the proposed research may be further explored along multiple dimensions to yield more comprehensive insights into the network. Specifically, we may investigate the integration of IRES in D2D communication systems using alternative surface types, and we may also study the effects of system parameter variations on the network performance. Finally, we may delve into the technical challenges associated with the design and implementation of IRES-assisted D2D communication systems. This study formulates a probability issue and derives its quantitative outcome for a $d$-dimensional lattice walk starting from the origin and adhering to the edges of a hypercube. The walk is said to succeed if it reaches a pre-defined destination. The primary objective is to determine the total number of successful walks. The approach employed involves converting the problem into a combinatorial challenge by subdividing the positive octant of the lattice into uniform sections, then developing an expression for the number of successful walks within each section. Ultimately, the total count of successful walks is obtained by summing the counts from all sections, thus generalizing a prior finding by Merkl and M\"oller for the $d=2$ case, and further extending a prior result by Curran for walks on the edges of a $d$-dimensional regular polytope. The derived formula is shown to be applicable to various geometric shapes, including the $d$-dimensional cube, the cross-polytope, the simplex, and the orthoplex, with specific results provided for $d=3$. The approach can be adapted to accommodate weighted walks by applying a Möbius inversion formula. The associated code for calculating walk counts in the $d$-dimensional cube has been publicly shared. The associated theory can be utilized for designing stochastic processes, and is related to a random stroll on the edges of a $d$-dimensional cube. The derived formulas can be utilized for creating a stochastic process, specifically a random stroll, which can be utilized as a building block for more intricate theoretical applications. We have investigated the thermal properties of doped graphene, focusing on its heat capacity, by considering the effects of electron-electron and electron-photon interactions. Our analysis revealed that these interactions generate a temperature-dependent shielding length that impacts the thermal behavior. Specifically, we discovered that the heat capacity exhibits linear temperature dependence when electron-electron interactions dominate and that this linear dependence can be reversed at very low temperatures due to electron-photon interactions. Notably, the heat capacity's temperature coefficient can be adjusted to be positive or negative by adjusting the density of doped graphene. Our theoretical findings are consistent with recent experimental observations. Graphene's unique thermal characteristics offer a unique platform to study quantum phenomena and develop novel technologies. The material's thermal behavior is influenced by quantum fluctuations and screening effects, which can be influenced by temperature and doping levels. By understanding these phenomena, we can harness them to develop groundbreaking technologies. Our work provides a theoretical framework that can inform and interpret experimental results. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the thermal shielding length is directly related to the phase shift of intervalley transitions, which is influenced by the electron-photon interaction. This relationship enables us to investigate the interplay between electron-electron and electron-photon interactions and their impact on thermal screening and the phase shift of intervalley transitions. Our analysis also sheds light on the role of electron-electron and electron-photon interactions in doped graphene and identifies the conditions necessary to achieve positive or negative heat capacity coefficients. Finally, our results are relevant to research on doped graphene and provide a theoretical framework for understanding the unique thermal screening properties of this material. Moreover, our analysis could facilitate the development of novel devices based on doped graphene that can harness and control quantum phenomena. Additionally, our results could inform and guide experimental research on doped graphene by providing a theoretical basis for understanding its thermal screening properties and interpreting experimental results. Finally, our analysis confirms that the heat capacity of doped graphene is sensitive to electron-electron and electron-photon interactions and that these interactions generate a temperature-dependent shielding length that impacts the thermal screening of the material. Our results are consistent with experimental data and provide a theoretical framework for understanding the thermal screening of doped graphene. By employing a double encoding network to represent spoken text in a manner sensitive to the speaker's tone, this approach has shown success in generating high-quality speech. Notably, the generated speech demonstrates a more pronounced emphasis on the speaker's characteristics. In addition, the system yields superior results compared to conventional speech synthesis methods, with a significant boost in speech quality for a limited amount of training data. The system's ability to focus on speaker-specific traits has been independently verified using disentangled speech representation. The proposed system is built upon the Flamingo neural model, which is primarily trained on a large dataset of dialogues. As such, it is capable of capturing the nuances of the speaker's voice, even when processing unseen sentences. To optimize performance, the system incorporates an optional classification mask that identifies spoken sections and blocks the masking approach, preserving the speaker's tone in the generated speech. A compact neural network is designed to make the same predictions as a larger model, by mapping a smaller space that's derived from the larger model's parameters. This is achieved through a simplified approach to predictive inference, which involves approximating latent variables under a specific condition. As a result, the modified algorithm reduces computation and memory requirements, especially when dealing with regression tasks in Bayesian neural networks. Our method can also be used to create more compact models and aid the removal of unnecessary neurons during sparse neural network development. Two types of mappings - linear and non-linear - are explored, along with the implementation of an efficient computational strategy to prevent performance degradation. Moreover, the research highlights that the success of the method depends on the stopping criterion used and the structure of the models under consideration. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm in both non-Bayesian and Bayesian neural network contexts. Specifically, the results show that the method maintains similar levels of accuracy while significantly decreasing the size of the models. Additionally, a comparison with existing sparsification techniques and model compression methods was conducted to further establish the credibility of the research. A version of this work was previously published in the arXiv '20, '21, '22 platforms and is now being formally published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research. Artificial intelligence and its associated technologies have become integral to daily life, with machine learning serving as a fundamental component. However, like conventional systems, machine learning is susceptible to manipulation and can be compromised by cunning attacks that exploit its reliance on input data. A specific type of threat involves adversaries interfering with data streams transmitted between applications, altering the content without modifying the communication framework. This study investigates novel attacks where an attacker positions themselves between the user and the machine learning classifier, allowing the manipulation of input data while appearing legitimate. Our research introduces two sophisticated attacks - data manipulation and data fabrication - demonstrating their significant impact on accuracy, with manipulation altering the classification result and fabrication entirely creating novel instances. Our data fabrication attack can be executed using generative adversarial networks, enabling the creation of entirely artificial samples that evade classification. Our analysis also includes an evaluation of three distinct machine learning algorithms - support vector machines, random forests, and convolutional neural networks - highlighting their varying vulnerabilities to this type of attack. A detailed analysis of our results reveals that the impact of these attacks varies based on the complexity of the input data and the specific machine learning method employed. Our work also compares the efficiency of the data manipulation attack against the data fabrication attack, showing that the latter can yield accuracy rates of 97% or higher with as few as 40 iterations. Our research also includes an exploration of potential countermeasures, including input validation and the use of authentic data, as well as a discussion of the limitations of our approach and potential avenues for further research. Our experiments are conducted within a Python-based framework and the corresponding code is publicly available on a dedicated GitHub repository. Our experiments demonstrate that machine learning can be compromised through the placement of an attacker between the user and the classifier, highlighting the need for future research in this domain. Additionally, our findings underscore the importance of employing robust machine learning methods that can resist manipulation and provide secure classifications even in the presence of compromised input data. Conversely, some machine learning algorithms may be inherently vulnerable to this type of attack, necessitating the use of alternative models and potential countermeasures to mitigate this risk. Our work contributes to a growing body of research on machine learning security, specifically exploring the consequences of insider threats and the manipulation of input data streams. Our novel attack approach can be applied to various machine learning applications beyond our study, while our findings also raise questions about the reliability of machine learning in general and whether such attacks could occur naturally. Our research has potential practical implications, as machine learning systems may be subject to similar attacks in real-world settings,

Climate change deniers on social media often promote alternative facts, such as attributing the cause of the cold weather to the Earth's rotation slowing down. To counter this, our approach involves identifying and addressing these myths through accurate climate information. First, we analyze user posts on Twitter to pinpoint instances of climate change denials accompanied by a perceived justification. Subsequently, we present scientifically substantiated refutations that also address potential misconceptions. To gauge the efficacy of these responses, we have devised a method of evaluating reframing, which assesses how social media users perceive and process them. Our responses have been framed as both direct rebukes and as persuasive arguments. Our study reveals that social media users predominantly view climate change-related responses, with or without misconceptions, as somewhat convincing. Conversely, online users view the Earth's rotation as an unreliable explanation for the weather with little conviction. Building on this, our strategy could serve as a model for addressing other myths spreading on social media. Our data and method are available for public use at https://github.com/ClimateMyths/ClimateMyths/tree/master/data. Our website climate.myths.org provides a live demonstration of our approach. Link prediction in knowledge graphs has been effectively applied in various tasks such as relation prediction, entity typing, and relation discovery. Current approaches to relation discovery have achieved success by leveraging additional supervision, yet this method is impractical due to the resource-intensive process of annotating data. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework that capitalizes on the potential of knowledge graph connection prediction to supplement relation discovery techniques. Our framework relies on the connection prediction information to filter and identify the most reliable relations among the candidate links, thereby enhancing the model's performance without requiring extra annotations. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on three datasets - Wikidata, YAGO, and NELL - which yield impressive results, with our method outperforming the baseline in relation discovery. Notably, when combined with the baseline approach, our strategy achieves a 21.1%, 15.2%, and 53.1% improvement in F1-score on the three datasets, respectively. The integration of these methods not only decreases the reliance on costly data annotation but also elevates the overall performance of relation discovery. The proposed method is model-agnostic, allowing the use of pre-existing models when possible, or the application of transfer learning with shared layers. We demonstrate its effectiveness in various settings, such as image classification, using the ImageNet dataset and the MNIST dataset, and showcase its adaptability across diverse domains. Furthermore, our method exhibits promising performance in other domain shift scenarios, such as the presence of inter-quadrant shifts in data. Deep learning methods have achieved remarkable success across various domains.
Despite their effectiveness, the underlying geometry of these algorithms is
still poorly understood. In our study, we delve into the geometric properties
of deep learning models, revealing that the composition of multiple layered
connections corresponds to a topological space with specific properties.
Our analysis demonstrates that deep learning models can be characterized by a
specific type of space known as a metrisable space, with the ability to
calculate metrics and Borel densities for the outputs. By mapping the input
to a higher-dimensional space, we can establish a relationship between the
input and output distributions, even in cases where the mapping is not
injective. Furthermore, we provide a unified framework for analyzing deep
learning geometric structures, enabling the exploration of diverse model
architectures and their corresponding training methods. By examining the
geometric properties of deep learning, we can gain insights into their behavior
and development of new algorithms. In particular, we apply our approach to
investigate the relationships between inputs, outputs, and representations
within neural networks. By probing these representations with structured
inputs, we can gain a deeper understanding of the structure of the data and
the learned representations. Ultimately, examining the geometric properties
of deep learning methods enables us to generate new questions and areas of
investigation. In particular, we explore the geometric implications of
differentially private regularization and the effects of gradient clipping. In
addition, we provide a geometric interpretation of the concept of information
flow in deep learning models and the role of activation functions in this
context. Additionally, we examine the geometric properties of variational
autoencoders and generative adversarial networks, including the sampling process
and the generated distributions. In contrast, we find that recurrent neural
networks and Markov chain Monte Carlo methods exhibit complex geometric properties
that are difficult to analyze. In the companion chapter, we delve into the
technical details of the geometric analysis of deep learning models. In the
companion chapter, we also examine the geometric properties of reinforcement
learning algorithms, including the relationship between states, actions, and
values. In the companion chapter, we explore the geometric properties of
generative learning models and examine their relationship with discriminative
learning models. Furthermore, we examine the geometric properties of
semi-supervised learning and how it relates to clustering and transcription
factor binding sites. In the companion chapter, we examine the geometric
properties of learning to propagate features in graph-structured data.

Let R be a ring (not necessarily a commutative ring) and I an ideal of R.
The qth L-depth of an element r in R is defined as the minimum number of elements that compose the ideal generated by r, which is the least number of elements in an expression of r as a sum of q elements from the ideal I.
The 0th L-depth of r is defined as 0.
Among the many properties of L-depth, a notable one is that it satisfies the weak exchange property.
In this study, we explore specific properties of the exchange property and the lattice of L-depths in particular.
We define a subset A of R as being chief if it is an exchange set when combined with the set of L-depths.
We demonstrate that chief elements possess unique properties and that the lattice of L-depths has a comprehensive ordering.
Furthermore, we establish the relationship between chief elements and the extremal elements of the lattice.
In addition, we present two separate methods for identifying the extremal elements as either monomial or non-monomial.
Finally, we examine the extremal elements in the context of a commutative ring and provide a computational example for illustration purposes.

Our understanding of how people perceive and interact with virtual environments is
essential for the development and application of virtual reality (VR) technology.
While the primary consideration is typically the high-quality visual and audio
presentations that engage users, another crucial aspect is often overlooked: the
projection of shadows. This projection not only enhances the visual realism of the
3D scene but also provides additional spatial information that can affect user
perception. By conducting a user study, we investigated the impact of shadow
aspects on VR experiences. First, we analyzed the system variables influencing
shadow quality, then we conducted a study with 245 participants to assess the
effect of shadow quality on user comfort and performance in a 3D task. Our
results demonstrate that shadow quality does indeed impact user experience,
contributing up to a 9% increase in comfort levels and a 5% performance decrease
for low quality. This outcome highlights the significance of shadow aspects in VR,
suggesting that systems with satisfactory shadow rendering can improve user
comfort while poorly rendered shadows may slightly hinder performance, and thus
this area remains an intriguing research space in the realm of VR psychology. By
opening this research space, we initiate the exploration of shadow-related mental
processes, setting the stage for future research to dig deeper into these processes
and ultimately unlock the potential of shadow psychology. Ultimately, our study
will contribute to creating more engaging and effective VR applications by addressing
the often-overlooked but crucial aspect of shadow rendering. Furthermore, we
provide a theoretical framework that can be applied to various research domains,
enabling researchers to follow our example and investigate the role of system
aspects like shadow quality in shaping user experience. By doing so, we can
generate more predictive models of user behavior and develop a deeper understanding
of how different system variables influence behavior in numerous application areas
beyond VR, such as human-computer interaction and social psychology. Finally, we
suggest possible applications of our research, such as using VR to recreate historical

Distortions in the cosmic microwave background's power spectrum can be effectively analyzed through a technique called XQC and PIMMS, which measure the distorted signal in the radial bispectrum. However, these methods have limitations and are only applicable under specific conditions. As a result, researchers have developed a new approach called the Distorting the CMB × LSS Bispectrum Examining Technique (DCLET). This method has several advantages over existing methods: it's faster, requires fewer assumptions, and is more versatile. DCLET involves calculating the distorted signal in the CMB's bispectrum using three different estimators and is capable of detecting spatially anisotropic distortions. Additionally, the technique can estimate the distorted signal even when the distortions are not negligible, a condition known as $\mathcal{F} < 1$. Our simulations indicate that DCLET is more efficient than existing methods and can provide accurate results within a short period. Specifically, DCLET can determine the distorted signal up to $k_{max} \sim 0.1$ h/Mpc in a 2D space within 10 hours, whereas existing methods can only reach $k_{max} \sim 0.05$ h/Mpc in a 2D space within the same time frame. However, our results also show that DCLET is sensitive to potential systematic errors and the accuracy of the CMB's power spectrum measurement. Future experiments with higher resolution and larger datasets will enable the detection of more subtle distortions. In particular, our analysis indicates that the upcoming PRISM satellite experiment will be capable of detecting a bias as low as $(\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln k}{\mathrm{d}\ln P_{\rm CMB}})_{\rm rad}\sim 10^{-3}$ at a 2$\sigma$ confidence level. Overall, DCLET represents an effective tool for detecting distortions in the CMB's power spectrum and will significantly contribute to upcoming experiments like PRISM and other satellite missions. Additionally, the technique can be adapted for use in spectroscopic surveys like the Roman Astronomical Instrument. In the case of DESI, our results show that DCLET can detect a bias as low as $(\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln k}{\mathrm{d}\ln P_{\rm CMB}})_{\rm rad}\sim 5\times 10^{-4}$ at a 2$\sigma$ confidence level. In summary, DCLET is a versatile technique that can effectively detect distortions

We develop a robust Bayesian estimation framework that can withstand malicious attacks. Our framework first derives adversarial tolerance criteria for parameter estimation, then formulates an optimization problem to minimize expected loss. By solving this optimization, we obtain a posterior distribution that can serve as a certificate of resilience, providing an upper bound on the impact of adversarial interference. Our framework is versatile, allowing various loss functions and both continuous and discrete problem settings. We examine a practical scenario, a frequency estimation problem, where an attacker seeks to distort measurements of a signal's power spectrum. Our framework proves effective in estimating frequencies even when the attacker aims to maximize distortion. Our framework also exhibits adaptive resilience, meaning its effectiveness can be adjusted based on the actual level of adversarial interference. Experimental results demonstrate that in the presence of adversaries, the robust Bayesian estimator exhibits reduced bias and enhanced variance compared to the traditional Bayesian estimator. Furthermore, the robust estimator exhibits improved computational efficiency. Our framework is further demonstrated through a real-world example, where we estimate a signal buried in noise from a spectrogram, while an adversary attempts to distort the spectrogram. Our framework proves to be highly effective in this scenario. Detailed mathematical analysis and comparisons with other robust estimation methods are also provided. This research has potential applications in a range of fields including navigation, audio processing, and medical diagnosis. The accuracy of molecular models is crucial for extracting reliable information, particularly when analyzing protein structures. Critical to achieving this accuracy is the representation of amide proton bond stiffness, which is essential for capturing long-range effects in quantum interactions. However, existing protein models often fail to account for this stiffness, leading to an incomplete understanding of molecular behavior. To address this limitation, a new approach is introduced, which validates and refines protein models by incorporating the quantum-derived frequencies of amide proton vibrations. This methodology, known as CPDISC, allows for the calculation of vibrational frequencies between pairs of atoms. By applying CPDISC to a comprehensive dataset of 102 amide hydrogen-containing peptides, the results demonstrate that incorporating vibrational frequencies into protein models yields a 10-fold improvement in the prediction of certain molecular characteristics. Furthermore, the integration of CPDISC-enabled terms into protein models, specifically through the use of machine learning-based parameterization, enhances the accuracy of molecular predictions, ultimately yielding a 15% improvement when compared to the standard GROMOS model. To facilitate the widespread adoption of CPDISC, the study includes detailed computational methods and provides access to the derived parameters through a publicly available repository. This approach is expected to contribute significantly to the advancement of molecular modeling, ultimately driving innovation in fields such as pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, and quantum computing. Additionally, CPDISC has the potential to be applied to other areas of physics and chemistry, expanding its utility beyond protein modeling. By applying quantum-derived principles to the analysis of NMR nOe, dePISD, and hydrogen-bonded scalar couplings, the results demonstrate that CPDISC can also inform the development of empirical potential terms, including van der Waals and electrostatic interactions. This finding suggests that CPDISC-enabled terms can be used to optimize the transfer of information between quantum-based and empirical protein models, ultimately yielding a more accurate and nuanced understanding of molecular behavior. A new approach is introduced, which applies the parquet approximation to calculate the density function of a Fermi surface. The parquet approximation is traditionally used within the context of density-functional theory but our method diverges from that framework. Instead, it combines elements from two sources: the Berezinskii model for quantum circuits and the Kotliarenko model for strongly interacting fermions. The density function of a Fermi surface is equivalent to a solution of a Bubnov equation, which can be transformed into a Berezinskii model. Solving this equation yields an analytical solution for the density function, which we refer to as the Kotliarenko solution. However, this solution is only exact in the limit of infinite particle number; when particle number is finite, it becomes a stochastic approximation. Despite its limitations, the Kotliarenko solution offers valuable insights, particularly its application in the Kotliarenko model, where it predicts a transition from a superfluid to a normal state. Similar predictions can be made for a Fermi surface, where it forecasts a transition from a Fermi liquid to a normal state. The parquet approximation also enables us to model interactions that are beyond the reach of density-functional theory, including attractive and repulsive interactions of any strength. The approach can be extended to include spin-orbit coupling and applied to study spin textures and other exotic phenomena. Finally, the Hamiltonian formulation of the parquet approximation offers a versatile tool for studying a wide range of many-body systems. The method can be applied to one-dimensional systems, where it predicts a transition from a Luttinger liquid to a normal state, and it also forecasts the emergence of topological phenomena in certain parquet diagrams. When designing computational systems to be playful, it's essential to achieve a balance of attributes that create an engaging and fun user experience. The concept of "illumination" in this context refers to the insight that these attributes work together harmoniously to generate computational playfulness. The underlying mathematical framework for this balance is provided by the fundamental theorem of calculus. We show that upper Smyth powerspaces preserve core-conciseness, leading to a strong result that core-conciseness is preserved under any weakly monotone lifting, thereby solving an issue raised in a previous study. Additionally, we define and investigate the concept of lower Smyth powerspaces, demonstrating that they are equivalent to the upper powerspace and preserve core-conciseness, similar to the original Smyth upper powerspace. Finally, we introduce the notion of half-core-conciseness for partial orders and examine its relationship with core-conciseness, ultimately showing its preservation by the Smyth T-topology for any given half-core-concise partial order. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of the mathematical theory of Smyth T-topology and its associated powerspaces. The study also provides a useful framework for the domain theory of programming languages, particularly in analysing the semantics of exceptions. The main findings of this research are applied in an examination of the core-conciseness of several programming languages, including ML, F\$, ML\*, F\*, and their respective exception-continuation semantics. The core-conciseness of these languages is determined by the relationship between their Smyth T-topology and their Scott topologies. Specifically, we find that ML and F\* have core-concise domains if and only if they have Scott core-concise domains, while ML\* and F\* preserve core-conciseness even when including exceptions in the program. The key insight underlying these results involves the identification of a lifting that relates the Scott topologies to the upper Smyth T-topologies, and the demonstration of core-conciseness for certain domain-theoretic constructs, including compactly aligned domains, domains with a compact decomposition, and domains that can be decomposed into a compact product domain. The core-conciseness of ML\* and F\* can also be attributed to the presence of a well-ordering that reflects the program's topological structure in its denotational semantics. Furthermore, we show that the core-conciseness of ML and F\* can be preserved if the program's control-flow graph is well-ordered topologically. The results presented in this research can be applied to give semantics-based justification for a range of program-transformation techniques, including the elimination of redundant exceptions, the folding of nested try-catch blocks, and the folding of nested block-delimited code. To estimate parameters in Bayesian models related to extreme value phenomena, a convenient choice is the mean of the posterior distribution within the unit interval [0,T]. The traditional parameterization, however, poses difficulties during the sampling process, as it results in uneven acceptance rates for parameters located at the boundaries. To mitigate these issues, a new approach is suggested, which transforms the original Poisson process to one with more manageable posterior analysis. The proposed method involves transforming the original parameters using a cumulative distribution function, resulting in parameters that behave symmetrically and facilitate efficient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling. The introduction of an easy-to-implement adaptive warming phase in this process further enhances sampling efficiency by dynamically adjusting the initial learning rate based on the median of the posterior's marginal distribution. The presented technique, therefore, enables the seamless generation of samples for a widely employed extreme value model, the CAPM-EV model, using the No-U-turn sampler. The technique's versatility allows it to be applied to various extreme value models as well as other Bayesian estimation contexts that rely on the mean of the posterior within a specified interval. In Offline Reinforcement Learning, it's often difficult to guarantee the data quality due to the data collection being separate from the learning process and potential corruption issues. We're the first to explore the concept of data-dependent corruption robustness in the context of offline RL. Our new performance metric measures how resilient corrupted datasets are, and we establish a boundary that combines both robust and efficient offline RL techniques. Notably, we introduce a novel approach that doesn't rely on the corruption distribution and can be applied even if the entire dataset is corrupted. This result also improves the existing offline RL performance, making our work distinct. Through experiments, especially in the domain of grid worlds, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our new approach and the significance of data-dependent corruption robustness. Additionally, we provide theoretical justification for our method and conduct thorough analyses to ensure its reliability. We also test our approach on real-world data from the AI2THOR simulator, where the results show a substantial improvement over the baseline offline RL method. Predictive modeling of infectious disease spread is crucial for an effective response, informing public health policies and resource allocation strategies to mitigate the pandemic's impact. To enhance the accuracy and timeliness of predictions, researchers are developing and refining individual-based modeling approaches that account for exposure risks shared by passengers on an urban bus network. To build upon this framework, this study undertakes a methodological clarification, highlighting the benefits of using a well-mixed model as a benchmark to evaluate individual-based models. By integrating the urban bus network and simulating the movement of individuals, the latter provides more precise predictions of infections. However, our analysis shows that the incremental gain in predictions comes at a cost, revealing the value of a well-mixed model as a simpler yet more computationally efficient alternative. Through a case study of Melbourne, Australia, our results demonstrate that a well-mixed model can reduce computational costs by up to 57% while still yielding predictions within 3% of those generated by the individual-based model. Given the computational demands of individual-based models, our findings make a significant contribution, paving the way for the development of more practical models that balance accuracy and computational complexity. A Double Faced Auction (DFA) is an online trading mechanism that allows buyers and sellers to bid on goods without knowing the actions of their competitors. Our research builds on this concept, taking into account the complexity of monetary transactions by incorporating a novel payment scheme. This payment method ensures that only successful trades result in payments, with funds transferred between parties by reversing the payment flow. Our mechanism, called Authenticated DFA (A-DFA), addresses the reliability issues of traditional DFA models, which may be vulnerable to cheating due to the ability to manipulate payments. By employing a trusted third-party arbiter and utilizing time-stamped transaction records, A-DFA mitigates the risk of fraudulent activity among participants. Our model relies on a ball-and-urn token management system, where the arbiter manages tokens, transferring them between buyers and sellers in accordance with bidding agreements. Our results indicate that A-DFA operates under a condition known as Weak Monotonicity, and we have developed an analytical framework to study the mechanism's performance. Using this framework, we have computed precise values for revenue and social welfare, which are commonly used evaluation metrics in auction theory. Furthermore, we have established a relationship between A-DFA and another payment mechanism, Revealed Preference Payment (RPP), allowing us to compare the outcomes under both scenarios. Our findings also suggest a relationship between the funds held by the arbiter, known as the funds' steady-state distribution. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that A-DFA yields superior outcomes in both revenue and social welfare compared to RPP, validating the use of A-DFA in time-sensitive trading applications where monetary transactions are involved. The benefits of A-DFA can be seen in its ability to minimize the funds held by the arbiter, resulting in lower operational costs for the mechanism. The novel payment scheme employed by A-DFA results in payments being reversed, thus preventing the accumulation of funds by the arbiter. Consequently, the choice between DFA and A-DFA depends on specific requirements and constraints of the application at hand, encompassing the need to mitigate cheating and operational costs. Our work presents an extension of DFA, addressing reliability issues and providing a mechanism that can effectively counter fraudulent activity. Conversely, in scenarios where payment manipulation is not a concern, DFA may yield superior outcomes due to its ability to provide precise revenue and social welfare values. The integration of a trusted third-party arbiter in A-DFA is essential in mitigating the risk of fraudulent activity, thus validating the use of this mechanism in various trading applications. Image-based recall systems have found success in various applications, but their potential in visual navigation tasks has remained unexplored. A recall system's ability to retrieve past observations is particularly beneficial for tasks that require traversing long paths or remembering specific scenes, like navigating an institution. However, retrieving all remembered images would be unnecessary and inefficient for these tasks. To address this, we introduce MemoNav, a novel approach that selects the most relevant memories for visual navigation by leveraging a simple transformer-based model. MemoNav relies on an image embedding technique that captures the essence of each recall, allowing it to choose memories that complement the agent's current view and guide it towards its target more effectively. We evaluate MemoNav's effectiveness in navigating various datasets, achieving superior performance compared to existing methods. Moreover, MemoNav's memory selection strategy enables more efficient recall usage, with results showing a density of 97.5% compared to 67.6% for the second best method. Additionally, MemoNav's ability to choose insightful memories reduces memory requirements by a factor of 2.9 compared to 5.0 for the second best method. These benefits enable MemoNav to succeed in tasks that would be challenging for traditional recall-based approaches. To facilitate reproducibility, our code and dataset are available for public access. Machine learning models are becoming increasingly essential in high-stakes decision-making processes, yet their reliability is often compromised by a lack of explanation and accountability. In contrast, legal professionals undergo rigorous training to develop argumentation skills, which involve presenting and justifying claims with supporting evidence. In contrast to the absolute certainty expected in a court of law, our work focuses on addressing decisions plagued by uncertainty - existing forest-based machine learning models cannot account for such ambiguities. We introduce Indecision Forests, a novel learning paradigm that combines argumentation with quantitative uncertainty, enabling it to be represented as a probability distribution over possible worlds. Our model achieves this by applying argumentation protocols to identify and weigh relevant evidence, which is then utilized to compute decision credibility. We demonstrate the capabilities of Indecision Forests through a series of case studies, including one that simulates a complex moral dilemma, showcasing its ability to tolerate and quantify ambiguity. Experimental results reveal that Indecision Forests can safely navigate cases of ambiguity, producing meaningful outcomes in up to 80% of cases while maintaining a level of uncertainty as high as 20%. This paper explores three agents with distinct approaches to climate action, representing the interests of current and future generations. We find that their interactions lead to stalemates, particularly when one agent prioritizes short-term gains and the other focuses on long-term sustainability. To break these impasses, we investigate the agents' willingness to make economic sacrifices in the name of environmental protection, revealing that the most effective approach involves the present generation taking collective action to address these issues. Our analysis also yields potential policy applications, including the use of carbon credits, which allow the present generation to make ecological amends while still acknowledging the needs of future generations. Ultimately, our model suggests that partnership and cooperation offer the most promising path forward in addressing global environmental challenges. Our work specifically examines the case study of the UK's carbon emissions, providing a framework for similar analyses in other countries and regions. We hope that this research will contribute to informed decision-making and foster a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between societal interests and environmental priorities. Our findings are particularly relevant during the current pandemic, as they shed light on the trade-offs between short-term and long-term health goals and the resulting distribution of burdens. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Climate-Economics/Climate-Policy/tree/main/Climate_Policy/Climate_Society_Partnership_Climate. This project forms part of the Climate Economics Group's research, and we would be delighted to receive feedback or input from other researchers. We especially invite contributions that can help expand our model to incorporate the complex societal dynamics driving climate action, as well as the distribution of pandemic-related burdens. For example, how might climate policy considerations intersect with the economic impacts of the pandemic, and what are the resulting distributional effects on different societal groups? Exploring these questions could lead to a richer understanding of the interplay between ecological and economic priorities, ultimately fostering more effective decision-making and cooperation across different agents. We look forward to engaging with other researchers and building on these ideas. We present a comprehensive English-language knowledge base, KSB, comprising a pair of lists: queries and responses. Each query represents an information-seeking inquiry, while the corresponding response mirrors the corresponding section title from a research study. The dataset encompasses 328 research-based queries and 328 corresponding responses, achieved through examination of 246 scientific papers across various disciplines. The initial 246 papers were selected from a broader dataset of 3,772 research studies, following a rigorous review process that identified a specific section type containing the sought-after information. Each paper was then analyzed to generate a query in the manner suggested by its corresponding section title. Notably, human annotators contributed to the dataset by offering alternative queries and responses, resulting in the adaptation of traditional knowledge graphs into query-response pairs. KSB can facilitate the training of conversational agents, while also serving as a benchmark to gauge their performance. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/leobora/KSB.

Calculating accurate object shapes from their shadows has been a critical task in both computer vision and graphics. While traditional methods rely on simulated shadows obtained through ray tracing, this approach is too slow for current applications. In contrast, learning-based methods that use simulated data have demonstrated high accuracy but require a substantial amount of simulated data, which can be costly to produce. We propose a new method that leverages differentiability to efficiently collect a vast amount of simulated data, allowing for more effective training. Our method involves using a simplified shape rendering technique that considers the object as a simple plane, and it achieves this while maintaining accuracy. This approach enables the development of highly accurate shape estimation tools that surpass previous methods. Our contributions include a novel and efficient shadow calculation algorithm, as well as a precise shape estimation method that can handle complex scenes with multiple objects. Ultimately, our method allows for seamless integration of simulated shadows into a differentiable rendering framework, thereby facilitating the rapid collection of a vast amount of annotated data. In addition to shape estimation, our framework also differentiates to address other inverse problems, such as recovering occluded regions and identifying superpixel segments within an image. The source code for these methods is publicly available.

Two well-known algorithms for generating random spanning trees are the Aldous-Broder method and Wilson's algorithm. Typically, the Aldous-Broder method is associated with a post-order traversal, whereas Wilson's algorithm is linked to a path-based exploration. Notably, there's a rare scenario where the two algorithms produce the same sequence of trees. We explore the conditions for this equivalence to occur and present a novel approach for generating random spanning trees. This approach can be broken down into two distinct phases, allowing for the integration of both algorithms in a unified manner. The first phase generates a preliminary spanning tree using the Aldous-Broder method or Wilson's algorithm. Subsequently, the second phase employs an efficient pruning procedure based on a pre-order traversal to reduce the size of the tree. To our knowledge, this two-phase framework has not been previously suggested in the existing literature. Furthermore, we suggest an improved pruning strategy that offers a time complexity of O(n log n) with n being the number of vertices. The benefits of this approach are that it allows for tree exploration while simultaneously sampling random spanning trees of varying sizes, thereby providing user flexibility to select a tree of a desired size. Additionally, we propose an extended version of the Wilson's algorithm that incorporates a size-control feature for generating random spanning arboles. The proposed framework has significant practical applications and can be used as a general method for sampling random spanning trees, spanning arboles, and arbitrary subgraphs within a variety of graph models including the E-R random graph model with edge probability p. Lastly, we examine the sampling efficiency of our proposed algorithm and demonstrate its potential for rapid convergence through statistical analysis and experimental results. One notable outcome is that the proposed algorithm yields an expected time complexity of O(n log n) for generating a random spanning tree, which is superior to existing algorithms with a complexity of O(n^2) or O(n^3 log n). Consequently, this algorithm presents an efficient solution to the graph sampling problem. The findings presented in this work are expected to contribute to the ongoing research in graph sampling and random spanning tree generation, thereby expanding the existing knowledge in this domain. When assessing how input parameters affect the output of complex systems, researchers often employ global sensitivity analysis. In the context of evolutionary algorithm (EA) hyperparameter research, this typically involves analyzing how different parameter choices impact fitness function values. Our investigation utilized the HS method to evaluate the sensitivity of 10 EA hyperparameters in 7 distinct permutation problems. The findings revealed that the most influential parameter positions varied depending on the specific problem and how the fitness function values changed. The results also showed that a parameter's significant impact was often indicated by a large range of effective values, as determined through sensitivity analysis. The investigation involved conducting 1000 runs for each combination of parameter and problem, and the sensitivity values were calculated using these fitness function values. The analysis involved examining the distribution of these values, as well as the correlation between these values and fitness function values, to quantify sensitivity. The analysis of these values enabled us to distinguish between direct and indirect effects on fitness function values. Our analysis demonstrated that indirect effects were more pronounced, and the primary driver of fitness function value differences was random variation. The analysis highlighted the challenge of interpreting sensitivity values, and future research will involve exploring ways to utilize global sensitivity analysis in EA hyperparameter research. The code used in this investigation is publicly available via the link provided. Additionally, the dataset containing sensitivity values has been made available for download. This article provides proof of well-known estimates for the wave equation in terms of $H^1$ and $\dot H^1$ norms, also incorporating a logarithmic correction as necessary. We discuss the implications of these estimates within the context of quantum mechanics. Specifically, we examine the behavior of solutions to the wave equation in relation to initial data measured by the Sobolev norm and its derivative, ultimately leading to the exploration of a priori bounds for Schrödinger evolution. This in turn allows us to investigate the properties of a related nonlocal operator, whose growth operator we ultimately establish. This nonlocal operator has significant ties to the fractional Schrödinger equation and its variants. Our discussion is primarily driven by the desire to understand the maximum kinetic energy of a quantum mechanical particle subject to an external potential and its connection to the fractional Hardy-Littlewood conjecture. We also examine the minimum regularity required for the wave equation's well-posedness, marked by the critical Sobolev exponent, and its implications in quantum mechanics. Throughout, we emphasize the distinct roles of the $H^1$ and $\dot H^1$ norms, highlighting their significance via a simple mechanical analogy. This article also serves as a comprehensive overview of the estimates associated with the wave equation, suitable for graduate students and researchers in mathematical physics and analysis. To facilitate this, we include a brief review of relevant operator theory at the beginning. We also consider a related problem, namely the recovery of an object's mass density from measurements of its surface's displacement, a problem with significant real-world applications. This problem is a standard one in inverse scattering, but it requires us to think differently about the usual phase space's time-reflected version. Instead, we are forced to focus on the wave equation's propagation operator, leading to a nonlocal characterization of the desired density in terms of the operator's potential. This in turn enables us to study the spectral properties of the operator, and to propose a feasible recovery method, and to estimate its error. This problem is a direct application of the wave equation's nonlocal behavior, and its consideration of the time-reflected version of phase space. This article also explores the optimal regularity of solutions to the wave equation, and examines the implications of enhancing the regularity via Fourier multipliers. This in turn enables us to study the most efficient way to propagate the wave equation's energy, and to examine the properties of a low-frequency filter. Two significant conditions, glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy, are identified through a single comprehensive eye examination utilizing our proposed framework, without the need for separate assessments. To effectively integrate information from different sources, we employ a dual-stream strategy, one for each type of data. This study proposes a novel approach to determining the severity of COVID-19 cases based on X-ray image analysis. The conventional severity assessment for COVID-19 patients primarily relies on two lung regions, the lower and upper lobes. However, our method considers four lobes to provide a more comprehensive evaluation. For each lobe, we identified three distinct sub-regions and employed a multi-task convolutional neural network to analyze features from these areas. By integrating the severity levels of all sub-regions, we can accurately calculate the overall severity of COVID-19 cases. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate that this four-lobe analysis produces better results compared to the existing double-lobe assessment. Furthermore, our research explores the characteristics of ICU admission by analyzing lung regions and discovers specific patterns. Additionally, we examined the diversity of the ICU dataset by calculating the mean and variance of severity levels for both the proposed four-lobe and traditional double-lobe assessment methods. The resulting variance of the four-lobe approach is significantly greater than that of the double-lobe method, indicating greater diversity with ICU admission. This dataset significantly surpasses currently available datasets in terms of size and complexity. To effectively engage in conversational activities, a chatbot must be able to pinpoint the underlying objectives behind user inputs. Yet, pinpointing these intents proves challenging due to their frequently ambiguous nature. Traditional approaches rely on assuming pre-defined intents with assigned labels for each, training the model to categorize inputs based on these objectives, and then assessing its performance using standard evaluation metrics. Nonetheless, this approach falls short in real-world applications, primarily because the pre-defined intents may not align with actual user goals and adapting to new, unforeseen intents becomes impractical. In response, our proposed method diverges from conventional techniques by eliminating the need to categorize inputs into pre-defined objectives. Instead, our model treats the labeling of intents as an unsupervised process, leveraging the chatbot's dialogue history and user feedback to self-identify the relevant objectives in an unsupervised manner. By doing so, our model enables several key advantages: 1) a more accurate representation of user goals, as the chatbot is able to self-define the objectives without external influence, 2) improved generalizability, as the chatbot is better equipped to handle objectives both known and unknown, and 3) enhanced conversational performance, as the chatbot is able to tailor its responses to the chat history and user feedback. Our model integrates elements from self-supervised learning and contrastive learning to enhance the chatbot's ability to distinguish between relevant and irrelevant objectives. Our chatbot also showcases superior conversational abilities in several key areas, including user engagement, conversational length, and overall conversational quality. This research introduces the Virtual Safe Framework, a novel, five-stage, five-component VLIW processor that securely handles both arithmetic and logical operations within Boolean circuits, ultimately supporting the execution of Python code via TinyCrypt, under the encryption of Microsoft's Homomorphic Encryption Library (MEHL). Each of the five stages – Encryption, Circuit Construction, Byte Splitting, Base Generation, and Decryption – is responsible for a specific function in the execution of encrypted code. A detailed performance analysis across different processor frequencies and MEHL versions reveals that VSAs reach 99% efficiency, outperforming both MEHL's built-in executor and a previous HyTE-based approach. Furthermore, VSFs achieve greater execution speeds than these compared systems, executing 44 to over 80 times more operations before encountering performance limitations. Specifically, VSFs can execute 50,000 to 140,000 additional processor cycles before becoming slow, enabled by the VSFs' ability to execute multiple evaluator operations in parallel. Ultimately, this innovation brings encrypted support for Python 3.6 within reach, marking a significant advancement over prior solutions. To facilitate further research, the VSFs' source code and supporting documents are freely accessible on a public GitHub repository. Additionally, the authors have documented their development process and outlined a step-by-step approach for replicating the Virtual Safe Framework. Lastly, to validate the reliability of the Virtual Safe Framework, as well as the security of the MEHL against potential attacks, the authors conducted and presented various validation tests, which are available for review on the same GitHub repository used to share the VSFs' open-source code. These validation tests, performed under controlled conditions, demonstrate the continued efficacy and reliability of the Virtual Safe Framework, in particular, and the MEHL, more broadly. To isolate any potential system-wide errors, these validation tests were conducted in an isolated, pure Python environment. In sum, the Virtual Safe Framework, as a fully customizable, five-component, VLIW processor, stands out as a leading solution for securely executing code within encrypted environments, offering greater efficiency, execution speeds, and a wider range of supported operations than prior solutions, while also ensuring the reliability of these results through rigorous validation tests. In the field of autonomous driving, environmental conditions such as fog and snow heavily impair a vehicle's ability to navigate. To improve safety, a vehicle must be able to adapt to these situations by utilizing information from multiple camera angles. Currently, most advanced autonomous vehicles rely on standard RGB cameras but struggle in harsh weather due to their limited spectral range. To overcome this limitation, vehicles equipped with hyperspectral cameras can capture more detailed spectral information. Despite the potential benefits, using this technology is hindered by the significant processing requirements involved. To address this, a new method is proposed that allows vehicles to prioritize processing based on critical sections of the image. Specifically, the vehicle identifies the most relevant pixels in each frame and creates a more manageable image based on these key pixels. By optimizing processing, vehicles can conserve energy and switch to alternative sensors when necessary. Our system is tested on a variety of scenarios, including real-world images, and demonstrates a processing time reduction of up to 90%. Additionally, vehicles equipped with this system are able to accurately interpret the environment even in conditions as low as 10% image clarity. Our results show that vehicles equipped with this capability can reliably switch to alternative sensors, such as LIDAR, even when it is partially obstructed by fog or snow. By improving sensor processing efficiency, vehicles are able to prioritize resources and stay within safety guidelines, such as processing 10 times faster than real-time to guarantee timely decision-making. Our research enables vehicles to better navigate a variety of environments and stay within safety regulations by utilizing multiple camera angles effectively. This study identifies constant-time executable operations by examining the bounded-time algorithm problem, leading to a key conclusion - an operation can be executed in constant time if and only if it doesn't require the computation of the division of two variables. Notably, this condition allows for constant-time multiplication despite the asymptotic non-constant time required to calculate the product of two n-bit numbers. To address this disparity, we introduce a concept called "almost linear" unitary systems and demonstrate their equivalence to a particular class of multilinear formulas, ultimately revealing the basic building blocks for constant-time execution. This leads to a constant-time algorithm for the all-pairs shortest paths problem with integer weights, but also highlights an unexpected challenge - obtaining constant-time output for a problem solved in linear time may be unachievable. To resolve this issue, we develop a notion called "preprocessing tolerance" and use it to distinguish between problems that can be solved efficiently with approximate solutions and those requiring precise solutions. This distinction enables us to obtain nearly optimal time complexities for several fundamental problems, including all-pairs shortest paths, minimum cost flow in undirected graphs, and bipartite matching. Furthermore, we obtain improved time complexities for finding the k minimum spanning trees and k vertex connected components. Finally, we explore the relationship between constant-time execution and multilinear formulas, particularly in the context of polynomials of specific degree. This leads to a conjecture stating that an operation can be executed in constant time only if it's multilinear in its input variables, which would have significant implications for the design of constant-time algorithms. Recommender systems are now incorporating session-based recommendation to address the limitations of traditional methods. Session-based recommendation systems address the "known item problem" by leveraging user behavior within each session. Since each session typically comprises only a few interactions, recommending items immediately after the user's last interaction within the session can enhance user experience and model performance. However, this poses a significant challenge for item recommendation, as well as for handling data imbalance and modeling for individual sessions and overall user behavior. To address these complexities, we introduce an innovative session-based recommender model that combines graph neural networks, a self-guided approach, and a co-training technique. Our approach is rooted in two interconnected concepts: (1) session orientation, which aims to capture the inherent characteristics of each user session using an undirected graph to connect items within each session, and (2) a two-stage learning process inspired by graph co-training. Our method involves initial training on one node type (e.g., user-item graphs) and subsequent refinement using information from another node type (e.g., item-item graphs), all with the aim of enhancing our model's robustness and performance. Our model is capable of processing long-term user preferences and can provide recommendations at the end of each session. We have conducted extensive experiments on public datasets, including the TripAdvisor, Yelp, and Amazon datasets, as well as two proprietary datasets. Our results demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms cutting-edge session-based recommender systems, including neural and embedding-based methods, in terms of accuracy, as our approach is uniquely positioned at the intersection of graph neural networks and co-training. Our model's performance is further highlighted by the novel sessions it can handle and its ability to balance item diversity and density. Our in-depth analysis and the accompanying code have been made publicly available, as well as two proprietary datasets, with the aim of facilitating future research in this area. Our model's performance is comparable to that of a theoretical baseline that uses information from the beginning to the end of each session. Our approach is also noteworthy as it is one of the few examples of successfully applying co-training to recommender systems. We investigate the effect of interactions on the non-Hermitian topological properties of one-dimensional systems, specifically those exhibiting zero-energy modes at the boundary. These interactions, which are one-dimensional and range-dependent, weaken the topological protection, ultimately eliminating the topological gap in the spectrum. This can occur even in the absence of fermion number conservation, as seen in our model systems featuring power-law and exponential decay of the Diminution interaction. The emergence of flat band phenomena and localization can be understood through this new type of interaction, as well as the presence of bound states both internally and externally. Notably, the absence of Hermiticity does not inherently cause chaos, as evident from our findings. Lastly, we outline potential avenues for experimental realization, including one-dimensional systems such as cold atoms in optical lattices and photonic waveguide arrays. Furthermore, we propose examining the two-dimensional case, as the principles underlying the one-dimensional system suggest the possibility of an entirely new class of non-Hermitian topological phases.

We examine special cases of complex Eisenstein series for $GL(n, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ associated with the standard parabolic subgroups and the unramified base change property from the perspective of intermediate spaces. Specifically, our analysis focuses on the actions of Hecke algebra elements on the spaces of Eisenstein series, their relations to irreducible constituents of the unramified principal series, and the combinations of matrix coefficients that vanish due to the unramified base change property. By considering the interplay between the Casselman-Shalika formula and the Rankin-Selmer convolution of automorphic and non-ramified adelic functions, we determine the expressions of certain Eisenstein series at generic points of their orbits under the action of Weyl groups. Our work is driven by the goal of understanding the linear independence of the set of irreducible automorphic functions, a concept initially explored by the first author in his doctoral research. Along the way, our discussion also touches upon the local and global aspects of the unramified base change property, as well as the connections between the Rankin-Selmer convolution and the completion of the Hecke algebra with respect to the selfadjoint cone. Ultimately, our analysis enables us to present an unambiguous listing of those irreducible automorphic functions that remain unmodified by the process of unramified base change. Additionally, our results provide a mathematical explanation for the concept of interbreeding groups as described in the work of Ginzburg and Soudry, a topic that we divide into theory and computation.
