A longstanding problem known as Turan's tetrahedron challenge, posed almost sixty years ago, has seen recent progress in its resolution. The question at its core is about the existence of certain three-intersection property in certain graphs of n vertices. The answer to this question is complex, as it depends on the specific metric used for its evaluation and the value of n. In the case of the $\ell_2$-metric, for example, it has been shown that there is a constant, c, such that a graph of n vertices will have the three-intersection property if and only if the following condition is met: the number of edges in the graph is greater than $cn^{3/2}$. This solution marks a significant advancement towards understanding the problem and represents a major achievement in the field of combinatorics. Furthermore, the methods employed in its derivation led to the development of new and interesting results in the study of extremal graphs of n vertices. On the other hand, in the case of the $\ell_\infty$-metric, a different threshold value of $n\log n$ has been identified for the existence of the three-intersection property. Similarly, in the case of the Hamming metric, a different threshold value of $n/\log n$ has been identified for the existence of the three-intersection property. The complexity of this problem is evident in its relationship with other prominent problems, such as Szemeredi's conjecture and the Erdos-Folkman theorem, whose solutions also exhibit similar thresholds. The methods employed in its derivation are based on an innovative approach that combines probabilistic techniques with precise calculations, using the properties of the specific metric in question. In the case of the $\ell_2$-metric, for example, a novel probabilistic method was employed, which involved the development of a new inequality, the "hypergeometric inequality". Similarly, in the case of the Hamming metric, a different approach was employed, which involved the development of a new recursive formula and the application of Fourier analysis. The results obtained in this research are considered to be the best known solutions to this problem and represent a significant advancement towards its complete resolution. a thorough evaluation of their performance across 11 open-source deep learning libraries.

unjustified assumptions about the data or networks.

recommendation system that can provide reliable guidance to deep learning practitioners. The code and

with other algorithms. The empirical evaluation of different algorithms and their configurations has

considerations, but also on empirical evidence and a thorough evaluation of the potential risks and

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both significant and difficult to do.
In this study, we examine the feasibility of using basic LSTM networks for sentiment
classification on Twitter. Our model is tested with three different feature sets of varying
significance, which are word-based, word-based with additional context, and binary token sets.
As a result, our model achieves a 0.88 AUC score when using the full context of Twitter words.
When using just the target tweet for analysis, our LSTM approach reaches a 0.83 AUC score.
Compared to other comparable models, our results demonstrate exceptionally high performance. 
Our research not only validates the effectiveness of LSTM networks for sentiment analysis
but also shows that using more words rather than less leads to better outcomes. 
Additionally, our model is found to be very resistant to data manipulation through word
substitutions, a common technique used to manipulate sentiment classification. 
Our findings also make Twitter sentiment assessment more accessible and efficient. 
Our work is the first to make Twitter sentiment assessment more accessible and efficient. 
Our code is now available on GitHub for public use at https://github.com/AbhishekSurani/LSTM_Twitter_Sentiment_Analysis. 
Our model is also capable of providing detailed, word-by-word sentiment assessments. 
This capability makes it possible to analyze complex emotional connections and contexts.
As a result, our model can be used to analyze a range of emotions and produce more accurate
outcomes in a range of settings, including but not limited to, product evaluation and political
analysis. Additionally, our model is suitable for natural language processing tasks beyond
sentiment analysis and can be adapted for various tasks.

A secure method of generating truly random digits is achieved by harnessing the inherent variability introduced by process fluctuations during the manufacturing of integrated circuits. While the extraction of random bits from SRAM cells has become a popular approach, it is hampered by the need for separate voltage supply lines. To overcome this limitation, we present a universal method, called TuRaN, that enables the extraction of random bits from SRAM cells without the necessity of additional voltage regulators. TuRaN works by reducing the standard SRAM voltage to a value below which the SRAM array becomes unstable. This reduction is accomplished through underscaling of the VDD supply line, allowing a single reference circuit to determine when the SRAM contents have reached a state of genuine randomness. As such, TuRaN facilitates the incorporation of a truly random number generator into a wide array of existing integrated circuits. Our experimental findings, derived from evaluations using 28nm and 40nm technology nodes, indicate that the SRAM volatility is directly correlated to the undervolting level, enabling the detection of random bits at a significantly lower cost and with a reduced area requirement compared to alternative methods. Finally, our evaluation board tests, where the SRAM array was subjected to various stress conditions over an extended period, have consistently shown that the undervolt-based approach yields the same level of randomness as the traditional method employing dual voltage supply lines. Consequently, the incorporation of TuRaN enables the creation of secure digital systems capable of reliably generating random numbers, while also reducing energy consumption through undervolting and thus lowering the overall power consumption. We examine the potential link between the complexity of architectural design and the effectiveness of feature representation in neural networks. Our study compares the complexity of various neural network features by quantifying their geometric relationships using topological measures. This comparison highlights how the simplicity of the features discovered by neural networks is often the result of several constraints, including the limitations of the data, the properties of the learning algorithm, and the complexity of the target task. Furthermore, we propose a new approach that allows us to incorporate geometric complexity as an additional regularization mechanism to control the simplicity of the learned features directly. Our framework, GeomLN, can be integrated into any existing neural network without modifying its architecture or loss function; it merely adjusts the learning process to prioritize features with more straightforward geometric relationships. As a result, GeomLN achieves improved performance in a variety of low-level vision tasks, particularly those that require identifying structured patterns or detecting specific objects. Overall, our research demonstrates that sophisticated machine learning algorithms like deep neural networks can produce effective feature representations by incorporating multiple factors that promote simplicity and transparency. Additionally, the analysis provides insights for the development of future learning algorithms and architectures that can be easily translated into expert systems with interpretable results. A novel approach for determining the Wilson coefficients of the semileptonic $B^0$ decay into $K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ is proposed, employing a Wilson coefficient-free, data-driven method to directly calculate one coefficient, $C_7^{\rm eff}$, from Wilson coefficient assumptions. A second coefficient, $C_9^{\rm eff}$, can be determined using a two-equation, two-variable, least-squares fit of hadronic decay parameters and the differential decay rate $q^2$. The method allows for Wilson coefficient extraction from this specific decay without assuming specific hadronic matrix elements. A crucial parameter in this method is the hadronic mass $K^{*0}$, which serves as a reference point for determining certain Wilson coefficients. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to provide an immediate, Wilson coefficient-independent assessment of Wilson coefficients based on experimental data, thereby facilitating fit results based on a single Wilson coefficient assumption. The standard model predictions for several hadronic parameters, such as $K^{*0}$ mass and the branching fraction and angular distributions of $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$, are provided for comparison. The Wilson coefficient values obtained using this method are in line with current understanding. Our investigation specifically compares the effects of augmentation on two types of evaluation: foreground and background accuracy, with the former focusing on note and pitch features and the latter centered on pitch and rhythm aspects. This concept is contrasted with existing methods, which focus on past mobility outcomes. Mathematical representations of the prospects and outcomes are developed and their relationships are established through a mathematical connection. The prospect's influence on the social welfare of a society is then evaluated using a Laplace welfare function, which suggests that the fair distribution of prospects is equivalent to minimizing the equal relative prospectivity, a concept similar to Atkinson's income equality measure. The equality relative prospectivity is further divided into two parts: the first represents the variation in prospects within the population, analogous to the income variation in the Laplace welfare function, and the second represents the imbalance in the distribution of prospects, uncovering a hidden aspect of the prospect's distribution. In order to investigate the characteristics of the equality relative prospectivity, a new family of probability distributions, the generalized beta variables, is developed and their properties, including the mean, variance, mode, and skewness, are analyzed. The findings are then applied to simulate the distribution of intergenerational mobility prospects and to examine how they change over time in the United States. The simulated distribution of the prospects is found to be asymmetric and leptokurtic, and is characterized by a mode that occurs halfway through the sequence of the population, making the concept of prospects useful for understanding social mobility. the constraints of superdeterminism need to be taken into account, limiting the 
range of these coefficients. Consequently, this raises questions about using 
the Wigner function within a low-energy quantum framework. Notably, a restricted 
set of coefficients gives rise to the statistics of bosonic particles, whereas 
a highly restricted set yields the statistics of fermions. While both of these 
situations may seem straightforward, they are actually quite peculiar, as they 
involve deriving unusual forms for the energy-momentum relation. In contrast, 
an intermediate set of coefficients yields fermionic-like behavior for particles 
with half-integral spin, as well as fermonic-like behavior for particles with 
integral spin. This unusual regime has not been explored before. An examination 
of this unexplored regime has revealed novel aspects, including the results of a
quantum phase transition analysis and an assessment of the parity's role in the

Mandelstam function. Lastly, a fundamental superdeterminism constraint has been 
relaxed, giving rise to the concept of locally superdeterministic theories and 
the possibility of a quantum phase transition that follows a distinct pattern.

boosted the efficiency of solving structured linear equations. This acceleration
has enabled researchers to solve equations even in the presence of noise, a task
previously considered unreliable. We investigate the resilience of these matrix

toughness' to measure their robustness. We evaluate various solvers for regularized
problem formulations and evaluate their space toughness across different noise
levels. Our analysis sheds light on the robustness of solvers and reveals their
performance under different conditions, ultimately suggesting the use of Tikhonov
regularization for its robustness in handling noisy data. We further extend the
concept of space toughness to solve phase retrieval problems, a critical task in
many applications including optical phase retrieval, and demonstrate its
effectiveness to evaluate the robustness of phase retrieval algorithms. Our code
is publicly available at https://github.com/ahsanamir/Space-Toughness. We have
also developed a user-friendly interface at https://amir-hassan.github.io/Space-
Toughness to facilitate the evaluation of robustness for other problem
formulations and algorithms. Our findings can be replicated by utilizing our code
and interface. We envision the concept of space toughness to serve as a guiding

Advanced vehicle control systems, such as those using sensor fusion and predictive modeling, are crucial for safe operation but can sometimes be compromised by faults like sensor malfunctions which could lead to catastrophic consequences. To mitigate this, an approach is needed that can detect and correct potential errors in advanced vehicle systems while ensuring the driver receives accurate information. This research proposes a method called Prognostic Safety Filter (PSF) that utilizes System Level Synthesis (SLS) to develop a reliable and fault-tolerant model for use in vehicle navigation. By employing the PSF, the vehicle's navigation system can bypass unreliable sensors and switch to the prognosticated ones, thus preventing faulty information from affecting the system. The benefits of this approach are discussed in detail, along with its relevance to various advanced vehicle applications. To illustrate the effectiveness of the PSF, a case study is performed using a predictive vehicle model based on the constanta method, which is then synthesized using SLS. The resulting design is analyzed and compared to existing fault-tolerance methods, showing improved performance. Finally, the advantages of this PSF design are demonstrated in simulation tests involving vehicle path planning and validation. This work is an extension of a previously published paper, "Prognostic Safety Filter for Advanced Vehicle Applications," which appeared in the 2021 IEEE 60th Conference on Decision and Control (CDC). In the context of decentralized machine learning, we consider a network where individual nodes share parameters to achieve a common goal, minimizing a shared objective function. To robustly accomplish this task, we'll examine an alternative approach, DR-DSGD, which will be compared to the standard DSGD method. Assuming that the local data distributions on each node are known in advance, the DR-DSGD algorithm allows nodes to adjust their model updates based on the relative distributions. Through theoretical analysis, we'll establish the convergence rate of DR-DSGD, as well as its performance on standard graph decentralized learning tasks, with our results showing improved resilience to distributional differences. To further enhance scalability, we'll also outline a simplified version, DR-DSGD-S, which makes fewer assumptions about the data distributions. Our experiments will demonstrate the benefits of DR-DSGD, both in simulated data and when applying it to image classification on a distributed dataset. This research paper examines the space of holomorphic functions, specifically those within the $H^2$ subset of the bi-disc. It delves into characterizing C-normal weighted composition operators, defining a C-normal weighted composition operator as a composition operator followed by a multiplication operator, with the latter being compact and adapted to a specific subgroup of bi-holomorphic mappings. Investigation of the C-normal weighted composition operators provides insight into the diversity of operations between compact and non-compact transformations within the context of $H^2$ mappings. Furthermore, the study proves that the class of C-normal weighted composition operators represents the largest set of operators that maintain the compactness property among the broader group of WCC operators. To support these findings, several key properties and characteristics of C-normal weighted composition operators were identified and verified. Additionally, the research constructs illustrative examples of C-normal and WC-composition operators on $H^2$, and explores potential connections with related operator groups such as WC and C-composition operators. Finally, the research investigates whether the classification of C-normal weighted composition operators can be extended to the more complex context of bi-disc functions that are square-integrable with phase. The outcome suggests that the distinction between C-normal and WC-composition operators may disappear when considering square-interable phase in the bi-disc context. Consequently, the research presents new knowledge on the behavior of WC-composition operators in this context, and offers a counterexample that challenges a previously conjectured hypothesis. Finally, the research identifies an area for further investigation, specifically the potential relationship between WC-composition operators and compact-to-compact mappings. To answer this question, several relevant theorems were proposed. Lastly, the research verifies that WC-composition operators do indeed represent a broader class of operators that includes both C-normal and compact multiplication operators, and offers a potential pathway for demonstrating the compactness of the composition operator as well. To achieve this goal, several strategies were suggested. The research also presents an open problem, specifically the challenge of classifying all compact multiplication operators that can be expressed as a composition followed by a multiplication operation. The outcome could potentially enable a comprehensive enumeration of all WC-composition operators, and offer valuable insights into their characteristics as compact, composition-based operators. To address this issue, several approaches were proposed. This paper introduces a new transformation-dependent poisson disk sampling method for representing point cloud models. In contrast to existing techniques that rely on a single transformation, this approach learns from two distinct geometric transformations to generate a unified and continuous representation of the cloud. The method is further enhanced with a novel smoothing strategy, yielding a compact output with preserved detail. The evaluation demonstrates that the proposed technique surpasses traditional methods in terms of reconstruction error and preserves more intricate details. Notably, this technique can be applied to both volumetric and surface representations of the cloud. The implementation is available online.

The model on the left undergoes two transformations: radial expansion and
rotation. The resulting point set is then passed through the learning stage,
generating a function that produces a continuous, connected representation (center
image). The function is applied to the original model to produce a simplified
model with reduced noise (right image). The smooth, detailed model can then be
reconstructed using the MPM algorithm after applying a smoothing filter in the
frequency domain.

The model consists of a 3D U-Net with a backbone of ResNet34, with the final block

point to the smooth, detailed model. This value is then used to remove noisy points
and inform a function that produces a continuous, connected point cloud model.

The function produces a value indicating the distance from a point to the smooth,
detail-rich model, with negative values indicating points that should be removed
due to being too far from the original surface (blue). The function also controls
the density of the point cloud model, with higher values indicating a denser
point cloud (red).

generating a function that produces a value indicating the distance from a point to

remaining points are then filtered using a Gaussian filter in the frequency

Hydrogen boride (HB2) exhibits exceptional electrical conductivity at room temperature, suggesting the possibility of high-temperature superconductivity. To clarify its electronic properties and the potential for superconductivity, we performed in-depth density functional theory and hybrid functional analyses. The results indicate that HB2 is a semi-metal with a multi-band structure, featuring a narrow energy gap at the Fermi level. Through the calculation of the electron-phonon coupling and superconducting properties, we found that HB2's critical temperature is approximately 8 K, limited by a relatively low phonon frequency. While HB2's stability under ambient conditions is uncertain, our study shows that even if it were stable, its superconducting properties would not surpass that of existing high-temperature superconductors. Nevertheless, our research identifies potential pathways for enhancing the superconducting performance of HB2 and related materials, such as hydrogen carbide (MC2), by adjusting their structural properties. Ultimately, our findings may guide the synthesis of new two-dimensional materials with exceptional electrical properties. Moreover, our research provides a theoretical framework for a comprehensive understanding of the electronic and superconducting properties of van der Waals materials, shedding light on their potential applications. By utilizing time-series data, a methodical approach identifies distinct behaviors in complex systems by analyzing changes in their patterns. This approach, known as state transition clustering, is typically achieved by manually creating a grid to divide the state-space, after which the system's responses to various stimuli are observed and grouped accordingly. However, adjusting the grid's parameters significantly affects the outcomes, and improving the method requires re-defining the clustering framework. Building on a previously introduced concept, where the transition space serves as a weight matrix, here we propose a new framework for state transition clustering that is grounded in network analysis. This approach, tested using synthetic data and compared to three other methods, has the benefit of reducing the influence of parameter variations and offering a more accurate representation of the system's behaviors. Furthermore, this approach enables the identification of multiple paths between two states, thereby providing more comprehensive insights into the system. Additionally, this method can be used for systems with limited time-series data, and is capable of supplementing limited theoretical information about the system. To validate the approach, it was applied to two real-world systems, including a non-linear mechanical model subjected to different levels of excitation and a power system with two generators and various operating scenarios. The results demonstrate the ability of this approach to reveal the system's underlying structure, the existence of multiple paths, and the relationship between the system's parameters and its behaviors. The findings also highlight potential pitfalls and areas for further improvement. Based on these outcomes, it is recommended that future developments prioritize utilizing the transition space to inform control design and restore the system to a stable state. Moreover, this approach offers novel insights into the system's structure, and provides a data-driven understanding of the relationship between the system's parameters and its behaviors. To conclude, this approach offers a valuable addition to existing state transition clustering methods, and enables the extraction of meaningful insights from time-series data to guide the development of advanced control systems. This essay offers an exposition of the calculus as developed by Leibniz and his followers, with a focus on the central role played by infinitesimal analysis. Three distinct approaches are employed to recount the history of calculus in the 17th and early 18th centuries. The first method draws on the work of Keister and Edwards, utilizing a real number framework, while the second draws on the work of Raphaël Mufford, utilizing a Fregean framework, and finally, the third draws on the work of Robin Leibowitz, utilizing a Husserlian framework. Each of these approaches provides a unique perspective on the calculus as it was understood during the Enlightenment. Furthermore, we contend that these different perspectives remain valid despite the prevailing view that the calculus of that era should be understood through the framework of Abraham Robinson's non-standard analysis. Additionally, we offer a novel interpretation of Leibniz's concept of the generative law, one which resonates with the views of Carnap and Husserl. This interpretation enables a distinction between two forms of Leibnizian calculus, a "conservative" form which adheres to traditional notions and a "progressive' form which pushes the boundaries of those notions. While conservative in nature, the infinitesimal method does not compromise the validity of Leibnizian calculus, and by contrast, the progressive method, which incorporates the concept of a generative law, offers a more comprehensive understanding of the calculus. Finally, we contend that despite the success of modern calculus, the conservative method remains a viable option for pedagogical purposes. Consequently, we propose a reversal of the prevailing view, one which holds that the calculus of Leibnizian era should be understood through the framework of modern calculus. Instead, we advocate for a reversal of the order, utilizing the calculus of Leibnizian era as a direct framework for understanding the calculus. In this regard, we draw on the works of Carnap, Husserl, and Heidegger, while also acknowledging the influence of Leibnizian calculus on the development of philosophy in the 20th and 21st centuries. Ultimately, we offer a defense of the generative law as a fundamental concept in the philosophy of mathematics and physics. Moreover, we contend that despite numerous challenges and criticisms, the concept of the generative law has persevered, a testament to its continued relevance and importance. Finally, we propose that the generative law, in its various interpretations, offers a unique philosophical perspective

We conduct a thorough examination of HI intensity mapping measurements using interferometric data to forecast the outcomes of upcoming large-scale experiments. Leveraging the disturbance theory, we develop precise predictions for the linear HII correlations on both large scales and in terms of frequency spacing. Our formulaic approach enables efficient computation, facilitating the simulation of future observatories' performance. Notably, we evaluate the impact of removing the galactic foregrounds on cross-power spectra, demonstrating that removal can substantially alter the estimated redshift distribution of the signal. The analysis utilizes simulated data resembling the performance of next-generation instruments, specifically the CHORD and PUMA projects, to demonstrate these interferometric predictions. These will serve as essential tools for informing the design of future HI intensity mapping experiments. Moreover, the findings on foreground removal effects will guide strategies for mitigating galactic emissions in upcoming observations. With our framework, we can quickly modify the predictions to align with the expectations of various experiments, making our code publicly available for that purpose. In the 1990s, Donald Knuth's "The Art of Computer Programming" was a major influence on modern computer science, yet it also raised more complex questions that were left unresolved. This talk will address two of these issues, which involve the concept of limitless dimension in the Omega function and the independence of computational operators, and will present new framework called the ZAX framework for the automatic design of algorithms. The talk will also introduce a novel method for constructing algorithms at the meta-level, and will provide a demonstration of this approach through the development of a machine learning technique called the predictive 0/1 Greedy Algorithm. The latter has been independently developed by two researchers, whose work will be presented in this talk. The analysis will focus on the algorithm's statistical properties, as well as its relationship to the greedy algorithm and the ladder on sparse polynomials, which are key concepts in combinatorial geometry. The talk will also explore the connection between the predictive 0/1 Greedy Algorithm and the Knuth-Morse sort, which is one of the most efficient sorting algorithms available today. The latter's efficiency has been proven through the use of the lattice-reduction algorithm, which is a fundamental tool in number theory. The relationship between these seemingly disparate concepts will be clarified through the presentation of joint work with T. Leinonen, T. Raita, and J. Tarhala. The talk will cover three distinct areas of research, which are closely linked by the ZAX framework: the development of universal learning algorithms from arbitrary datasets, the design of packing algorithms for various geometric shapes, and the analysis of universal algorithms under the limiting condition. The latter concept is a key idea developed by A. Kolmogorov, who also proposed the initial framework for the design of universal algorithms. The latter's ideas will be discussed in detail, along with the work of numerous researchers who have contributed to this field, including P. Gao, T. Chan, and A. Chintala. The basic concept of observing a property in a system over time has been revisited by providing a detailed mathematical treatment in terms of (pre)exhaustiveness and uniqueness properties of time-abstracted systems. This involves defining and identifying the characteristics of different system representations, such as representations that abstract time or merge time-adjacent system states. Building on these properties, the observability of a system's temporal characteristics can be established. Specifically, the notion of first occurrence of a property is analyzed, and an algebraic procedure is developed to determine when two system representations preserve this property. Moreover, the relationship between system representations is examined in terms of (pre)exhaustiveness and uniqueness, and the conditions under which these representations preserve temporal properties are investigated. Finally, the results are applied to widely used system representations, such as automata, transition systems, and Markov decision processes, by demonstrating that the uniqueness of their representations is sufficient for observing temporal properties in these models. However, the necessity of such representations is illustrated through counterexamples. Finally, the observability of p-finite-word properties is investigated in time-abstracted systems, and the resulting theory is applied to the established concepts of time-bounded and time-constrained properties. This revisited analysis provides a comprehensive mathematical foundation for observing temporal properties in discrete-time systems and enables the development of algorithms for verifying time-bounded and time-constrained properties. Moreover, the results are translated into guidelines for designing such algorithms. Specifically, the theory is applied to the verification of properties in finite-state systems, and the resulting algorithms are demonstrated to be more efficient than existing methods for the verification of p-finite-word properties. Moreover, the theory is applied to the analysis of Markov decision processes by developing new algorithms for determining whether a property is time-bounded or time-constrained, and these algorithms are demonstrated to be more efficient than existing methods. Finally, the results are applied to the investigation of the complexity of observing temporal properties, and the observability of a property in a system over time is linked to the complexity of its verifier. Notably, the study reveals that the observability of a property in a Markov decision process is linked to its complexity of analysis (polynomial, co-NP-complete, or solvable only by a Turing machine), depending on the property under consideration. Moreover, the study examines the factors influencing the complexity of verifiers and observes temporal properties, and it demonstrates that these factors are highly dependent on the choice of system representation. The $k$-center problem is a classic clustering application with a well-defined metric space and a specified limit for cluster radius. When the graph of this problem is doubled, the radius of each point doubles as well, resulting in a new set of cluster centers. In contrast, the 'highway' measure considers the minimum number of doublings required for two randomly selected points to be within a certain distance of each other. Recent research aimed to reduce the time complexity of the $k$-center problem by using the highway property, leading to the $k$-center with the highway (KCH) variant. However, we demonstrate that the KCH variant cannot be reduced to the standard $k$-center problem, even with an increased approximation ratio. We also propose an algorithm for the KCH variant with an improved approximation ratio and outline its connection to the standard $k$-center problem through the doubling property. Specifically, the KCH variant with a certain approximation ratio can be applied to the standard $k$-center problem with a related, albeit slightly worse approximation ratio. We confirm that our results, including a particular time complexity, are previously unseen and represent the optimal performance for the KCH variant with the standard parameters. We investigate the problem of network scale estimation in small-world graphs in the presence of malicious nodes that can deceive other nodes with incorrect information. Each node initiates the process by gathering its local network metrics, after which they concurrently run a distributed algorithm to compute an estimate of the graph's size. To achieve this, we establish a minimum requirement for the algorithm's information exchange and design a new protocol that allows accurate scale estimation despite up to $n^{0.342}$ malicious nodes for large networks, where $n$ represents the network size. For smaller networks, our protocol can handle a proportionally greater number of malicious nodes. Both the algorithm's information exchange requirements and the protocol itself are engineered to be robust against malicious activities without relying on a central authority or a multi-layer communication process. Our results are based on a mathematical model of random graphs, specifically the Watts-Strogatz graph, which is a classic example of a small-world graph. Furthermore, our approach provides an estimated scale within a logarithmic factor of the actual size. Additionally, we analyze the algorithm's time complexity and asymptotic efficiency. Our findings include a protocol that can detect the presence of malicious nodes, allowing the algorithm to converge to a accurate scale estimation. To achieve this, our approach employs techniques like distributed voting, malicious node detection, and the verification of provided information, all of which are novel in the context of graph scale estimation. Finally, our work includes a detailed examination of the algorithm's metrics under the mentioned graph model, revealing that our approach is accurate and providing a comprehensive understanding of our results. Moreover, our protocol can be easily adapted for use in other graph models, and our findings include a discussion on the effects of varying parameters like the Watts-Strogatz parameter and the number of nodes and edges in a graph. Ultimately, our approach is designed to be efficient, allowing a low communication overhead and enabling accurate scale estimation even in large networks. To achieve this, our algorithm is engineered to minimize the amount of information exchanged between nodes. As a result, our approach is suitable for a wide range of applications, and our findings include a comparison of our algorithm to other distributed algorithms for graph scale estimation. Furthermore, our work is characterized by a lack of assumptions about the malicious nodes' behavior, making our approach strong against any possible malicious activity. Additionally, our protocol is designed such that the algorithm's information exchange is robust against various types of malicious activities. Finally, our work includes a discussion on the scalability of our approach and its potential applications to other problems in the distributed algorithm domain.

Numerical relativity, a highly complex field of study, relies on advanced computational methods to model gravitational wave emissions from binary black hole mergers. The most effective approach, using numerical solutions to Einstein's equations, is hampered by significant data requirements and limitations. A new method, referred to as the continued Hamiltonian evolution approach, offers an alternative solution that expands upon previous research. This approach simplifies data storage needs and enables more efficient use of memory, allowing for greater flexibility and computational speed. In contrast to traditional methods, the continued Hamiltonian evolution approach only requires storage of a lower amount of data, making numerical solutions more feasible. This approach expands the scope of numerical solutions that can be accurately modeled, enabling the study of more intricate systems and phenomena. Specifically, the continued Hamiltonian evolution approach enables the precise calculation of gravitational wave emissions for systems where the fluid approximation is valid, a previously intractable problem due to stringent data requirements. In addition to this advancement, the approach also offers additional benefits that facilitate the accurate long-term calculation of gravitational wave emissions. This includes the elimination of spurious high-frequency components and the accurate capture of semi-soft collapse regimes. As a result, the continued Hamiltonian evolution approach enables the long-term calculation of gravitational wave emissions, a major breakthrough in numerical relativity. This approach has been successfully implemented and tested in various simulations, including those involving binary black hole systems and collapsing fluid configurations. The findings from these simulations have been compared against existing numerical solutions and found to be in agreement. Notably, the long-term gravitational wave emissions calculated using the continued Hamiltonian evolution approach were found to be in precise alignment with previous analytical predictions. This approach represents a significant advancement in numerical relativity and has far-reaching implications for future computational modeling of binary black hole mergers and other complex gravitational systems. In particular, the continued Hamiltonian evolution approach offers a computationally efficient and efficient method for calculating late-time gravitational wave emissions, a major research objective in numerical relativity. The approach's efficiency enables the long-term calculation of gravitational wave emissions, a major research objective in numerical relativity. The main objective of the JUNO experiment is to monitor the neutrino oscillation parameter $\theta_{13}$ and verify the intermediate-scale mixing hypothesis by observing the $8^9$ keV anti-neutrino signal from $\beta\beta$ decay in $^{76}$Ge. To achieve this goal, a large, 20-inch photomultiplier tube is used to detect the $Ci$-like scintillator reactions within the 35-meter tall, 20-meter diameter, and 3-meter thick, water-filled tank that houses the detector. When conducting a meta-analysis with the goal of estimating individual study mean differences while accounting for within-study correlations, the typical approach encounters a problem. The issue arises because estimated mean differences are tied to variance-covariance parameters that are usually considered unknown. As a result, the estimated mean differences become functionally dependent on the estimated covariance parameters, ultimately resulting in unreliable confidence intervals. A novel class of estimators, called "cluster-stable" estimators, provides a solution to this problem by utilizing known within-study information to eliminate the need for covariance parameter estimation. We introduce two such estimators, the naive predictor and the shrinkage predictor, both of which demonstrate superior performance in comparison to alternative methods. The proposed estimators not only offer improved accuracy but also more accurate confidence intervals, as evidenced by our empirical findings and theoretical support. The benefits of these estimators were further highlighted in a real-world application using data from the sczmeta package, related to schizophrenia treatment data. The proposed approach also has broader applications in the field of meta-analysis. This work outlines a plan to enhance the accuracy of spectroscopic classification using machine learning and template-matching techniques, specifically for certain difficult-to-distinguish star types in the Gaia survey. We propose using advanced image processing methods on low-resolution spectrograms to mitigate potential biases and improve the accuracy of these techniques. We suggest three possible approaches: applying a data augmentation technique to the spectra before using them in machine learning models, using a model that can handle out-of-distribution data, such as Gaussian Process Regressors, and employing a method that can extract features from spectra that are more informative for the task at hand, such as wavelet transform. We expect these "astrophotonic" remedies to contribute to more accurate classifications of distinct stellar types. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in a case study involving the differentiation of M-dwarf stars based on spectral features. Our approach, incorporating wavelet transform and Gaussian Process Regressors, achieved an accuracy of 95.9% in distinguishing M-dwarf and Hertzsprung-Russell type stars, surpassing the baseline accuracy of 88.3%. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of these methods to improve other classification tasks in the Gaia dataset, such as distinguishing different stellar populations in color-magnitude diagrams. We provide a Python package called astrophotonics that implements the methods outlined in this work, allowing for the accurate classification of various stellar objects. We expect this package to be a valuable resource for researchers and scientists working with spectroscopic data. We welcome contributions and suggestions to improve the package, which we plan to maintain and update in the future. The code for the project is available at https://github.com/eduardo-rosa/astrophotonics. A copy of this work is available at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48550/arXiv.2207.07930. We outline our future plans in Section 4, and conclude this work in Section 5. We acknowledge the support that made this research possible in Section 6. When multiple medications are taken simultaneously, known as polypharmacy, there's a heightened risk of adverse drug interactions. To minimize harm, it's crucial to assess how different medications might interact when prescribed together. Although machine learning has been applied in this field to varying degrees, there's a notable absence of comprehensive reviews on the topic. Consequently, there's a lack of consistency in how medication interactions are represented and modeled. To address this issue, this paper offers a unified viewpoint on the application of machine learning in studying medication interactions. By examining the key concepts and models, a classification framework is established and evaluated, leading to an analysis of its strengths and weaknesses. Ultimately, this review aims to inspire advanced approaches that combine multiple learning techniques for a more detailed understanding of medication interactions. To this end, a case study involving a complex neural network-based model is presented that evaluates new medication combinations using existing data on drug relationships. Our work is made available on GitHub, allowing for replication of our results. Our temporary website for more information is at http://matt.szel.sztaki.hu/MDP.html. Experimental findings confirm the efficacy of our proposed model in accurately predicting adverse medication combinations while outperforming existing models in predicting both safe and hazardous polypharmacy combinations. The medication safety evaluation is currently in its infancy, and our work contributes to the development of a more cohesive relational deep learning framework that can effectively evaluate medication interactions and provide valuable insights for enhancing healthcare. As a result, the application of machine learning in this field will continue to evolve and contribute to the development of more sophisticated models that utilize relational data to predict medication interactions. Moreover, our model's ability to model two-way relationships between medications enhances our understanding of drug interactions and could be adapted for other complex classification tasks. A major uncertainty in theoretical stellar populations lies in the initial conditions of stellar formation, particularly how the protostar's internal structure influences the surrounding disk's fragmentation.  We have created a simplified model of a Population III star's internal structure, incorporating a strongly magnetic field.  By integrating this model into cosmological simulations of a star-forming region, we have obtained a detailed picture of the magnetic field dynamics and its effect on the disk around the protostar.  Contrary to previous studies, our results show that a strongly magnetized disk prevents the protostar's internal instability from causing the disk to fragment.  This outcome occurs because the magnetorotational instability is eliminated and the disk's angular momentum is efficiently removed through magnetohydrodynamic forces, resulting in a cooled and fragmented disk that matches recent observations.  Our research confirms that a strongly magnetized environment can prevent the disk's fragmentation, thereby refuting previous predictions of massive population III binary or multiple star formation.  However, our findings also suggest that a more realistic and complex internal star structure may yield a low-frequency instability that could fragment the disk and lead to binary or multiple star formation.  Additionally, our study highlights the necessity of using realistic initial mass fractions for accurate simulations of stellar formation.  Finally, we note that a strongly magnetized disk may result in an extended and fragmented disk that could be observable using the James Webb Space Telescope.  This could provide a rare opportunity to verify population III binary or multiple star formation models through observational evidence.  Such verification could help refine our theoretical understanding of stellar populations and may ultimately clarify the universe's initial conditions.  This could have significant implications for the development of stellar astrophysics.  By combining our findings with recent breakthroughs in both theory and observation, we may be on the verge of a major advancement in understanding the universe's initial conditions.  This could help resolve lingering uncertainties in stellar astrophysics and may enable us to infer information about the universe's initial conditions based on the present-day stellar population.  This could potentially allow us to look back further in time, thereby expanding our understanding of the universe's initial conditions. The formula enables the calculation of variances and expectations in both directions and can be applied to determine the optimal blend composition. Achieving genuine data privacy with sensitive information has driven the development of differential privacy. To address issues with previous methods that did not adequately protect against dependent information, a one-sided approach was introduced. This approach, however, has been found to be ineffective in certain situations, notably in the case of the mean of dependent values. This link prediction task is crucial for maintaining the accuracy and consistency of the knowledge graph as it grows, and is applied in a range of applications including spam detection and knowledge graph completion. To accelerate link prediction, researchers have proposed the concept of pre-training, pre-training the model using a large, publicly available knowledge base before fine-tuning it using a specific task and dataset. Pre-training has been shown to significantly speed up training and enhance performance when combined with tailored fine-tuning. In this research, we examine the potential of utilizing a fixed model for link prediction across multiple and diverse knowledge bases without the need for pre-training or continuous model adjustment. The model is trained and optimized using a large, openly accessible knowledge base, and our results indicate that it is capable of accurately predicting links in numerous knowledge bases, and outperforms methods that rely on tailored models and fine-tuning. Specifically, our results show that the model predicts approximately 80% of missing links in the knowledge base with high accuracy, and our work may contribute to the development of more efficient and scalable link prediction methods. Additionally, we propose a simple technique to enhance the model's performance, and our research may be applied to a range of knowledge bases including DBpedia, Wikidata, and YAGO. The code and knowledge graphs used in this research are publicly available for reproducibility. With further development, this approach may be adapted for use in knowledge graph-based applications such as question answering and semantic information retrieval. The knowledge graphs used in this research are listed below: YAGO, DBpedia, NELL, UML, YAGO, Freebase, and Wikidata. The fixed model's performance is compared to models that rely on pre-training and fine-tuning, and our results indicate that it is capable of accurately predicting links across multiple knowledge bases. The model's simplicity and potential for scalability make it an attractive alternative to existing link prediction methods. The code used in this research is publicly available for reproducibility. Inquiry answer selection, a key task in Question Answering on Scientific Knowledge Graphs, requires identifying appropriate responses to posed questions, with each inquiry linked to a set of validated knowledge graph triples. To tackle this challenge, we've developed a novel approach, incorporating external knowledge graph inference to inform language models. Our proposed method, TriInfer, leverages three different inference techniques - Transitive Inference, Predictive Inference, and Composite Inference - to enhance language model performance. Building on this framework, we integrated TriInfer with BERT and RoBERTa, resulting in the TriInfer-BERT and TriInfer-RoBERTa models. Experimental evaluations revealed that TriInfer-BERT and TriInfer-RoBERTa significantly outperformed the respective baseline models, with the improvement most pronounced on datasets with stronger graph connectivity. Moreover, by applying TriInfer to existing fine-tuned BERT and RoBERTa models, we achieved notable gains without incurring additional training costs. Consequently, this innovative approach has significant implications for enhancing the performance of language models on inquiry answer selection and related tasks. The implemented models and associated code have been made publicly available. Additionally, we have published a detailed guide on how to replicate the results and set up the models. We introduce a groundbreaking approach to developing new dimensionality expansions by utilizing covers of sets A and B. Under specific conditions, our method enables the creation of high-quality approximations for functions f(A, x) and f(x, B), which can be expressed as infinite series based on a measure θ(x). Notably, our methodology allows for the construction of more accurate approximation series when the measure θ is not absolutely convergent, thereby surpassing the limitations of traditional dimensionality expansions.

Our approach leads to the formulation of two novel high dimensional expansion theorems. The first theorem applies to functions f(A, x) that are subharmonics with respect to A, while the second theorem covers functions f(x, B) that are subharmonics with respect to B. By leveraging these theorems, we derive high dimensional expansion theorems for specific groups, including semigroups, rings, abelian groups, and certain finite groups.

Furthermore, our method facilitates the derivation of high dimensional expansion theorems for functions f(A, x) and f(x, B) that are superharmonics with respect to A or B, thereby marking a significant contribution to the existing literature. Additionally, our approach enables the development of high dimensional expansion theorems for functions f(A, x) and f(x, B) that are bounded, thereby demonstrating the approximation of these functions as infinite series based on a measure θ(x). 

The novel high dimensional expansion theorems derived in this study can be utilized to analyze a range of mathematical objects, including Cayley graphs, direct products, and certain infinite groups. Moreover, our results can be applied to examine the spectral gaps of these graphs. For instance, we provide an estimate for the spectral gap of the Cayley graph (Z_p)^3 with generators {((1, 2, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1)), ((1, 0, 2), (0, 0, 1), (2, 0, 0))}, which yields a spectral gap of at least 1 - (599/800). The techniques employed in this study can also be utilized to analyze superharmonic functions, including those related to the Heisenberg group and a specific infinite group with a 3-generator presentation. Lastly, our results are accompanied by a range of examples and counterexamples. One notable counterexample involves the infinite group with a 3-generator presentation defined by the word 'abaab'.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) magnetic patterns is crucial for in situ monitoring of spin dynamics in a diverse range of materials, particularly those with antiferromagnetic properties. Overcoming the challenges of modern magnetic characterization requires the development of more advanced and sensitive techniques. Our research demonstrates the deep learning-enhanced detection of intricate MW patterns using a single Rydberg atom, allowing for the identification of multiple frequency components within a broad MW spectrum. By using a model based on 2D convolutional neural Networks (CNN), we can analyze atomic spectra and extract information about the frequencies, amplitudes, and phases of MW fields. Notably, our findings show that even with limited atomic measurements, the CNN model can accurately reconstruct the MW spectrum. Moreover, we can optimize the atomic observation time to match the temporal evolution of MW changes, thereby enhancing our detection sensitivity. This improvement leads to a significant enhancement of our sensitivity, enabling the detection of MW fields about 25 times weaker than those detectable through conventional Rydberg detection methods. Our research presents a groundbreaking, in situ MW measurement technique that could revolutionize the monitoring of spin dynamics in materials with minimal disruption. Our study sets a new benchmark for the detection of MW fields, achieving the best results to date. Ultimately, this technique could facilitate a deeper understanding of the complex magnetic phenomena inherent in materials with antiferromagnetic properties. Additionally, our research provides a novel approach to extracting information from atomic spectra, opening up new avenues for application. A recent study analyzed 252 galaxies from the MaNGA survey to determine their disc stability. The findings revealed that disc stability decreases in galaxies with higher star formation rates and specific star populations. The $J/\psi$ signal identification process involved examining dimuon candidates with rapidities in the range of $3.76<y<4.26$, utilizing data obtained from the ALICE forward spectrometer. This new measurement is compared to theoretical predictions from both EPS05 and NRQCD models, considering different $k_T$ cuts and photon-nucleon luminosity functions. Additionally, the measured cross-section was combined with an earlier measurement made using the ALICE detector, yielding a combined result that is presented in this paper. The presented cross-section values are accurate to two significant digits and represent the measured $J/\psi$ production rates for both inclusive and direct interactions, as well as for those interactions that are influenced by photon-nucleon interactions, specifically those that are coherent and incoherent. The measured cross-section values were further analyzed and found to be in agreement with two distinct theoretical models, specifically the EPS05 and the NRQCD model, over a rapidity range of approximately three units. We address the challenge of encoding temporal information within sequential data,
utilizing recurrent architectures like GRU and GRU* as initially proposed.
Subsequently, we introduce two novel variants, GRU** and GRU***, of the above
architectures, which are designed to capture temporal relationships in a sequential
context.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our models through applications in knowledge
acquisition, specifically by re-ranking knowledge graph elements based on temporal
information, and present supporting evidence from our experiments. Additionally,
we introduce a new evaluation metric, End-2-End Performance, to comprehensively assess
the temporal awareness of our models. Our analysis compares the performance of the
four recurrent architectures, as well as the benefits of employing temporal feature
encoding, using a re-ranking approach for KBC tasks. Our results showcase the
advantages of our proposed models, particularly GRU** and GRU***, in various KBC
settings. The source code for our work is publicly accessible on GitHub.

These measures have economic consequences, including lost productivity and the cost of support for those in isolation or quarantine. We aim to minimize the total cost, in both dollars and human life, by optimizing the duration and type of countermeasure. To this end, we employ a novel computational strategy, searching for the best results by interacting with an oracle. The oracle supplies information about the most effective time to take action, given the current epidemic parameters. We demonstrate that this approach yields universally beneficial outcomes, regardless of the epidemic dynamics, and that these results can be applied widely to various countermeasures, including those used during the COVID-19 pandemic. The oracle's output also sheds light on a well-known phenomenon in which the optimal moment to take action coincides with the epidemic peak. Furthermore, our approach enables the exploration of previously unexamined countermeasures, such as those used simultaneously or in alternating sequences. The combined strategy proves to be both economically efficient and epidemic-management effective. Machine learning model performance can be compromised by data issues, with limited understanding of how specific data entities affect the model. To address this, we developed a data troubleshooting framework that uses the Shapley value to allocate responsibility for model performance among individual data items. Our framework also includes a method to identify crucial subsets of data and pinpoint specific records influencing the model. By employing this framework on real-world problems, such as identifying defective images in medical diagnosis and defective samples in vehicle inspection, we demonstrated its effectiveness and uncovered new insights. The proposed approach offers a novel and systematic means of quantifying data influence, thereby facilitating better data quality management and more targeted data maintenance activities. Critical data items can then be promptly rectified to maintain the overall quality of the data set. Moreover, this approach enables us to forecast model performance as data evolves and allows for the detection of data drift, thereby informing proactive data updating strategies to safeguard model reliability. Experimental results validate the accuracy of our approach and highlight the benefits of employing this framework for end-to-end machine learning applications. The associated code and dataset are accessible for public use. Our findings also suggest several avenues for further investigation. Firstly, the influence of data can be subject to variations based on different model architectures. This research focuses on how pressure affects the anomalous Hall effect in the triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn. Our initial findings reveal that at pressures below 35 GPa, the normal Hall effect persists, yet above this threshold, a significant transverse Hall resistance emerges, characteristic of materials lacking inversion symmetry. Through neutron diffraction, we established that the higher-pressure phase exhibits a structurally equivalent hexagonal arrangement to the initial phase, yet featuring significantly increased interatomic distances. Our computational models indicate that this structural modification facilitates the conversion of Mn sites from nearly equivalent to distinctly bonded, thereby stabilizing a long-range hexagonal order. Our data demonstrate that the emergence of the transverse Hall effect is directly correlated with the degree of bond regulation within the material's lattice at higher pressures, with our simulations suggesting that the material's spin arrangement is accountable for this phenomenon through the preservation of time-reversal symmetry. Our study provides valuable insights into the delicate interplay between magnetic arrangement and electronic properties in Mn$_3$Sn, offering a framework to understand the anomalous Hall effect in similar materials exhibiting magnetic triangles. Additionally, we have observed that when the material is in a liquid state at high pressures, the anomalous Hall effect is significantly reduced, yet still present, underscoring the importance of considering thermal motion in such phenomena. Our research also raises questions about the occurrence of complete hexagonal ordering in Mn, a topic that warrants further investigation. Finally, our results have sparked discussions on the potential coexistence of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic states at high pressures, an area that requires further exploration. Textile images exhibit unique characteristics due to the irregularities in their texture, resulting in diverse visual effects that are difficult to replicate through digital manipulation. While this uniqueness makes textile products more appealing, it also poses significant challenges for processing these images. Notably, distinguishing between authentic and synthetic textures is a crucial task. Most existing methods focus on analyzing texture macro-features, but this approach falls short in differentiating between genuine and fabricated textures. In contrast, this study proposes an innovative technique by analyzing micro-texture features in a localized context. Specifically, we employ the Generalized HOG operator to capture the intricate details in textile images, which are subsequently decomposed using low-rank matrix factorization to identify any anomalies. By recognizing that natural textures typically exhibit low rank, we aim to separate the noise and flaws in textile image data. Our method is designed to be flexible and can be applied to various textile flaw detection applications, such as identifying defects in textile products or detecting counterfeit clothing. the efficient use of agent evaluations. To overcome this issue, we have developed an
optimised emulator of text-based games, capable of processing millions of moves per
second. The TextWorldExpress emulator employs an array data structure and specific algorithms
to significantly enhance processing speed, with noticeable effects on agent training and
testing. For instance, agent training can be completed in a matter of minutes rather than
days, while agent evaluations can be completed in a matter of seconds rather than minutes. We
have made the TextWorldExpress emulator publicly available to facilitate research and
agent development. Additionally, we have conducted a comprehensive study to compare the
performance of various agent architectures using the classic text-based game, Treasure Hunt. 
The results show that certain agent architectures are better suited to specific game elements,
while a newly developed agent architecture outperforms existing ones in multiple evaluation
criteria. The code for TextWorldExpress, along with the data from our study, is openly
available at https://github.com/epfml/textworld_express. Further details on our approach
and research outcomes can be found in the accompanying paper. To evaluate the effectiveness
of our agent architectures, we have developed a range of challenging game modifications,
along with corresponding evaluation criteria and benchmarks, which can also be found on the
github repository. These resources can be used by the research community to develop and assess
new agent architectures, as well as to reproduce our study and compare the performance of
different agent architectures on various game modifications. To facilitate agent development
and evaluations, we have created a publicly accessible online platform, allowing users to
create custom text-based games, upload their agent designs and run evaluations, and access
pre-trained agents, all without requiring programming skills. The details for accessing this
online platform can also be found on the github repository. Finally, a summary of our approach
and research outcomes, along with the necessary information for reproducing our study, can be
found in a publicly available document, also available on the github repository.

Achieving complete control over high-energy attosecond pulses is crucial for capturing the initial stages of electron dynamics in its absolute temporal framework. The production of isolated high-energy attosecond pulses (IHPA) through a laser-driven plasma arc process appears to be the most feasible approach for attosecond metrology applications. However, the variability in plasma conditions may compromise the coherence properties of the pulses produced, rendering them inoperable for coherent manipulation techniques. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel scheme utilizing a robust-field two-color laser scheme to create IHPA, ensuring the preservation of pulse coherence and the viability of subsequent coherent manipulations. Numerical simulations demonstrate the creation of IHPAs with 50-as duration and an order of magnitude higher intensity than previously reported, along with an adjustable ratio of harmonics. The implementation of coherent manipulations yields pulses with controlled temporal gaps, lasting several hundred attoseconds. The proposed source of IHPAs has the potential to revolutionize the field of attosecond metrology by providing a reliable, coherent, and highly manipulable IHPA for studying electron dynamics and coherent extreme ultraviolet amplification. Additionally, it may contribute to the development of next-generation, laser-driven, table-top soft X-ray sources. Its implementation could significantly enhance the manipulation and utilization of IHPAs in various areas such as attosecond electronics, electron imaging, and coherent IHPA-based spectroscopy, and could even facilitate the creation of attosecond ICP lasers for bulk nonlinear manipulation of electron dynamics in solids. Furthermore, it may serve as a transient soft X-ray laser driver for coherent IHPA amplification in a subsequent gas medium, enabling the development of a fully coherent IHPA amplifier and revolutionizing the field of tabletop laser source development. Moreover, it could be employed as a transient soft X-ray emitter in X-ray microscopy and ICP-x-ray emission spectroscopy, and its implementation could greatly accelerate the development of highly coherent IHPA sources. Finally, it may be utilized as a transient soft X-ray emitter in X-ray quantum flash lamps and soft X-ray lasing, and its implementation could greatly accelerate the development of highly coherent IHPA lasers. Additionally, it could be utilized as a transient soft X-ray emitter in X-ray quantum lasing. The transient soft X-ray emission could be realized through either free-electron lasing or by transferring the energy of hot electrons to a heavy absorber, and it could be employed in XRL and other applications. The analysis reveals that the NC behavior near the ferroelectric/insulator interface is predominantly influenced by the steep slope of the ferroelectric hysteresis loop and not by the insulator's dielectric constant. By manipulating the ferroelectric material's properties, it is possible to control the onset of NC, thereby optimizing the MFIS structure's electrostatic response. The computational model developed in this work can be utilized to efficiently simulate the MFIS behavior, eliminating the need for time-consuming device simulations that incorporate quantum mechanical effects. Machine learning models' reliability is severely compromised when infected with malicious backdoors, specifically "trojan attacks". Traditional backdoors require the model to produce an incorrect output for a specific input, typically from a specific host, and correct outputs for other inputs. However, a more sophisticated type of backdoor, the "trojan assault", doesn't simply produce incorrect outputs, but also overconfident outputs, through the manipulation of confidence values. Moreover, a particularly challenging subcategory of this threat, the "host-free" type of backdoor, renders existing detection methods ineffective, as they rely on assumptions about the model's host. This paper introduces a new detection method, SHOTA, hostless trojan assault detection, designed to counteract this type of threat. It does so by analyzing the model's output distribution, rather than relying on specific input-output pairs or model parameters. Our method is both efficient and effective, as evidenced by its performance across multiple datasets, and it even surpasses the performance of existing detection methods, even those that utilize host information. Additionally, we propose a countermeasure, backdoor neural collapse, to prevent such threats altogether. The success of the exoplanet search program at the Observatoire de Haute-Provence has led to the identification of several terrestrial planets orbiting low-mass stars. To enhance the understanding of these planets' properties, we analyzed the elemental abundance of several suitable host stars. Notably, we developed a new approach for estimating the metal enrichment of these stars, which enables us to compare them to the solar value with greater precision. Combining our metallicity measurements with the mass-radius relationships of these planets, we inferred the theoretical density or core size of six gasless terrestrial planets. Our analysis revealed that four of these planets likely possess substantial cores, similar to those of Earth and Mars. However, two of these planets appear to have significantly smaller cores, suggesting they might be characterized by other distinct geological features. To construct habitats on other planets, building materials must be able to withstand extreme conditions found on Mars and the Moon, such as temperature fluctuations between -173 and 127 degrees Celsius. A comprehensive study was conducted to analyze how different temperatures affect the 3D printing process and the resulting structures. The study used electron microscopes to examine the microstructure of the Martian and Lunar regolith and how it changes with temperature. The findings showed that the optimal printing temperature is between 75 to 90 degrees Celsius, as temperatures below this point cause the soil particles to stick together too much, while higher temperatures cause them to expand and lose their adhesive properties. A pressing test revealed that the best mechanical strength is achieved between 75 to 90 degrees Celsius, with a slight improvement at 85 degrees. The study concluded that the optimal printing temperature is between 75 to 90 degrees Celsius, making this technique suitable for use on both Mars and the Moon. The constructed samples demonstrate remarkable durability and are resistant to various types of stress, making them an ideal material for habitat construction on other planets. The findings of this study will contribute to the development of sustainable and resource-efficient construction methods that can be used in extraterrestrial environments. The research also laid the groundwork for a novel type of 3D printing that can be adapted for use on other planets and moons in our solar system. The team is now working on developing new types of 3D printing techniques that can be used on other celestial bodies, as well as on Earth, using the native soil as a feedstock. The project is ongoing, with the researchers focusing on developing printing methods that can be used in low-gravity environments and exploring new applications for 3D printing on other planets. Assessment of the developed system was conducted through a test involving ten participants, who performed five practice sessions and provided accurate recognitions for the generated expressions. The proposed system's recognition performance has been documented for various expression lengths and types. Additionally, a method for automatically generating training data has been explored, utilizing three distinct approaches that can produce sensor data for mathematical expressions. This allows the system to be trained without the need for actual whiteboard recordings, thereby simplifying the training process. Overall, the recognition accuracy of the system was found to be high at 94%, with a average time complexity of O(n), where n represents the number of parts in the expression. The system's efficiency was further enhanced by employing a weight-based representation for the recognition of mathematical expressions, with the option to revert to a standard representation for comparison purposes. The developed system holds promise for applications such as intelligent mathematical expression assistants and could be further optimized through the incorporation of a neural network for even better performance. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, to capture more accurate dynamics, we model these events on hypergraphs, allowing individuals to interact with multiple groups at once. To find the threshold below which an epidemic will inevitably spread and that above which it will inevitably subside, we analyze a stochastic model on these hypergraphs. By assuming that transmission rates vary widely while average degrees remain relatively constant, we derive a precise extinction threshold. This threshold is expressed as the smallest eigenvalue of a certain matrix associated with the hypergraph. Additionally, we calculate the spectral limits for this matrix, providing a more detailed analysis near its smallest eigenvalue and initiating a broader investigation of these limits and their applications. Our methods also yield techniques for estimating the rapidity and likelihood of an epidemic's spread, giving rise to a new area of research within network epidemiology. As a testament to the validity of our approach, our simulations accurately predict the outcomes of complex disease transmissions on hypergraphs. These predictions are in line with existing research within the field. By applying our techniques to real-world scenarios, such as the spread of COVID-19 at a cruise ship, we demonstrate the potential for more refined modeling, leading to more precise and accurate forecasts. Ultimately, our work paves the way for improved and evidence-driven decision-making in the event of future epidemics. To facilitate replication and further investigation, our code and simulation data are openly accessible online. We employ a mean-field approach to study the magnetic properties of a bilayer of chromium trihalide, a 2D ferromagnet with a centrosymmetric structure. Using in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields, we investigate the anisotropy of the magnetic responses and the associated spin patterns. A weak field produces a non-linear response due to the intralayer exchange enhancement, while a strong field generates an odd symmetry component in the magnetization, alongside a linear in-plane response. Introducing a Rashba effect or a non-abundant chiral crystallographic structure influences the magnetic responses and their patterns. A Rashba effect causes an imbalance in the magnetic responses to in-plane and out-of-plane fields, while a chiral structure generates a spin Hall effect by producing a curved current path and amplifies the odd symmetry component of the magnetization. A Rashba effect also introduces a layer polarization in the presence of a chiral structure. We also examine the influence of a Rashba effect on the magnetic domain walls and find it is minimal compared to the effect of the exchange interaction. A strong chiral structure-induced Rashba effect leads to an imbalanced magnetic response to in-plane and out-of-plane fields and introduces a persistent transverse current even in the absence of a chiral crystallographic structure. A rationally designed chiral structure with a low symmetry is necessary to achieve this behavior. A Rashba effect also introduces a layer polarization in the presence of a strong chiral structure.
